matters.summary: The Federal Election Commission's Matter Under Review 7519 ("ARIZONA DEMOCRATIC PARTY") named Katie Hobbs as a respondent; the Commission's disposition for that respondent was "No Reason to Believe".

matters.title: FEC MUR 6888: REPUBLICAN NATIONAL COMMITTEE, ETAL
matters.summary: The Federal Election Commission's Matter Under Review 6888 ("REPUBLICAN NATIONAL COMMITTEE, ETAL") named Kelly Ayotte as a respondent; the Commission's disposition for that respondent was "No Reason to Believe".

matters.title: Ethics board review of taxpayer-funded COVID-19 ads under self-promotion law
matters.summary: Board unanimously found the governor did not violate the 2018 law barring statewide officials from using public funds for self-promotion.
matters.authority: Iowa Ethics and Campaign Disclosure Board

matters.title: State audit: federal COVID relief funds used for governor's staff salaries
matters.summary: Audit found about $450,000 in federal coronavirus relief funds paid 21 governor's office staff salaries in 2020 via the state homeland security department. The governor's office said the expense was justified.

matters.title: Ethics board complaints over donor-provided private flights dismissed; Court of Appeals upheld dismissal of challenge
matters.summary: The Iowa ethics board dismissed complaints in 2018 about flights on donors' private planes reported as in-kind campaign contributions. Attorney Gary Dickey's challenge was dismissed in court and, per AP in September 2019, the Iowa Court of Appeals upheld the dismissal.
matters.authority: Iowa Ethics and Campaign Disclosure Board; Iowa Court of Appeals

matters.title: Ethics board finds COVID-19 ad appearances did not violate self-promotion law
matters.summary: Following a State Auditor report, the board voted unanimously on 12 Aug 2021 that the governor's appearances in state COVID-19 safety ads did not violate the state's self-promotion statute.
matters.authority: Iowa Ethics and Campaign Disclosure Board

matters.title: Ethics board dismisses complaints on in-kind private flights accepted by Gov. Reynolds and her campaign (2018 IECDB 22 and 27)
matters.summary: The board unanimously dismissed two complaints that questioned whether Governor Reynolds violated the gift law and whether her campaign properly accepted, valued and reported nine in-kind flights. It found the flights legitimate in-kind contributions allowed under the gift law and the complaints legally insufficient.
matters.authority: Iowa Ethics and Campaign Disclosure Board
matters.penalty: None

matters.title: Ethics board finds no violation of self-promotion law in Gov. Reynolds' appearance in state COVID-19 ad campaign
matters.summary: After State Auditor Rob Sand's June 2021 report argued her appearance in the 'Step Up, Stop the Spread' ads funded with federal relief money broke a 2018 ban on public-funds self-promotion, the board voted unanimously that she did not violate the law, citing the pandemic emergency exception.
matters.authority: Iowa Ethics and Campaign Disclosure Board
matters.penalty: None

matters.title: Committee filed a report concluding no knowing violation by the Members and decided no further action was required.
matters.summary: Official record: Statement of the Chairman and Ranking Member of the Committee on Ethics Regarding Officially-Connected Travel to Azerbaijan in 2013

matters.title: OCE referral 15-2786: In May 2013, Representative Lujan Grisham traveled to Turkey and Baku, Azerbaijan.
matters.summary: In May 2013, Representative Lujan Grisham traveled to Turkey and Baku, Azerbaijan. Committee action: Procedural Objection (initial: Procedural Objection).

matters.title: State Ethics Commission settlement over cancellation of the Turquoise Care Medicaid RFP
matters.summary: On April 20, 2023 the Commission contended that cancelling the Turquoise Care RFP (Jan. 30, 2023) violated the NM Procurement Code and authorized a civil enforcement action naming the Governor and the Human Services Department. The parties settled after mediation on Aug. 10, 2023. The Governor denied all allegations and the agreement states it is not an admission of wrongdoing or liability.
matters.penalty: No monetary penalty stated. HSD agreed to rescind the January 30, 2023 termination notice and issue notices of intent to award to the four selected offerors.

matters.title: FEC MUR 8107: failure to properly disclose loans by Mike Braun for Indiana (Senate committee)
matters.summary: Following an FEC audit referral, the Commission found reason to believe the committee failed to properly disclose loans and accepted a pre-probable-cause conciliation agreement 6-0. Respondent was the campaign committee and its treasurer, not Braun personally.
matters.penalty: $159,000 civil penalty (conciliation agreement)

matters.title: FEC MUR 7490: complaint over 48-hour notice of candidate loan (Braun and committee)
matters.summary: Complaint by John Zody alleged reporting failures on a candidate loan. The Commission voted 4-0 to dismiss under its prosecutorial discretion; closed as to all respondents, including Braun.

matters.title: FEC MUR 7490: MIKE BRAUN FOR INDIANA
matters.summary: The Federal Election Commission's Matter Under Review 7490 ("MIKE BRAUN FOR INDIANA") named Mike Braun as a respondent; the Commission's disposition for that respondent was "Dismiss Pursuant to Prosecutorial Discretion".

matters.title: Executive Branch Ethics Act complaints over state-funded mailers and ads
matters.summary: Three ethics complaints about publicly funded mailers/ads were resolved by settlement under which Dunleavy reimbursed the state $2,800. The settlement was not an admission of wrongdoing; he stated he did not believe he violated the Act.
matters.authority: Alaska Personnel Board (independent counsel John Tiemessen)
matters.penalty: $2,800 reimbursement to the state

matters.title: Alaska Executive Branch Ethics Act complaints over state-funded advertising, settled with Personnel Board independent counsel
matters.summary: Complaints dated July 12, July 22 and August 18, 2019 alleged the Office of the Governor used State funds for partisan political advertising. A settlement agreement with Governor Dunleavy was signed Sept 4, 2020. Independent counsel found circumstances supported an inference that certain communications naming two officeholders had a partisan political purpose, attributed to inadequate education rather than improper intent; most communications were agreed not to violate the Act. The Governor stated he did not know of the communications before they were sent and does not believe he violated the Act.
matters.authority: Alaska Personnel Board (Independent Counsel John J. Tiemessen)
matters.penalty: $2,800 reimbursement to the State, stated not to be a fine or penalty; staff ethics training; no admission of wrongdoing

matters.title: State Ethics Commission consent order on 2010 campaign donor reporting
matters.summary: Gov. Haley agreed to pay a $3,500 fine and received a public warning from the South Carolina State Ethics Commission under a consent order, reported 2013-07-15, resolving a July 2011 complaint that her 2010 campaign filings omitted donor addresses and occupations. The commission's investigation found the campaign had addresses on file for all but eight donors.
matters.penalty: $3,500 fine and public warning

matters.title: South Carolina State Ethics Commission consent order over 2010 campaign donor disclosure
matters.summary: A July 2011 complaint cited 2010 gubernatorial campaign filings missing donor addresses and occupations. The Commission found probable cause in March 2012 and the matter was resolved by a consent order signed July 15, 2013 in lieu of a public hearing. The ethics.sc.gov resolved-complaints archive lists a 'HALEY, NIKKI' case 2012-003.
matters.penalty: $3,500 fine; $2,000 reimbursement of investigation costs; about $4,200 from eight donors forwarded to the Children's Trust Fund; public warning

matters.title: South Carolina House Ethics Committee complaint (Rainey) over conduct as a state representative
matters.summary: A complaint by John Rainey alleged ethics violations while she served in the state House, concerning her fundraising work for Lexington Medical Center and consulting for an engineering firm with state contracts. The committee voted 5-1 to dismiss all charges, saying there was not enough evidence of a rules violation.
matters.authority: South Carolina House of Representatives Ethics Committee

matters.title: Rainey v. Haley, South Carolina Supreme Court (civil ethics suit over conduct as a state representative)
matters.summary: John Rainey sued seeking a declaration that she violated the State Ethics Act as a House member. The circuit court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction and the Supreme Court affirmed, holding the House Ethics Committee has exclusive authority over such complaints. The court did not rule on the allegations.
matters.authority: Supreme Court of South Carolina (Opinion No. 27269)

matters.title: Lawyer Disciplinary Board complaint over Cardinal Health conflict of interest (as Attorney General)
matters.summary: A Milton business owner alleged an incurable conflict of interest in Morrisey's handling of the state's lawsuit against Cardinal Health. The Lawyer Disciplinary Board determined he did not break ethics rules; he had recused himself from the case in 2013. Resolution month approximate (reported January 2016 as 'last month').

matters.title: Lawyer Disciplinary Board complaint alleging conflict of interest in drug-distributor lawsuits
matters.summary: A Milton business owner's 2014 complaint said Morrisey, as Attorney General, could not fairly pursue Cardinal Health because of his earlier lobbying and his wife's lobbying for that company. The Board determined he did not break any ethics rules; he had recused himself from the Cardinal Health case in 2013. The Charleston Gazette-Mail reported the order also strongly warned him about conflict-of-interest duties. Reported January 2016.
matters.authority: West Virginia Lawyer Disciplinary Board (investigative panel)

matters.title: Vermont State Ethics Commission advisory opinion on financial ties to DuBois Construction
matters.summary: The commission issued an advisory opinion that Scott, as creditor of DuBois Construction (which does business with the state, after he sold his stake), had a conflict of interest. The commission has no enforcement powers; no penalty was imposed.

matters.title: MAGA Inc. ethics complaint alleging a shadow presidential campaign, book advance and travel
matters.summary: The Florida Commission on Ethics dismissed a complaint filed by the pro-Trump super PAC MAGA Inc. against Gov. DeSantis for lack of legal sufficiency, without opening its own investigation. Filing and ruling dates are approximate (filed March 2023; ruling reported 1 May 2023).

matters.title: Florida Commission on Ethics dismisses MAGA Inc. complaint over alleged 'shadow presidential campaign'
matters.summary: The Florida Commission on Ethics dismissed a complaint filed by the pro-Trump PAC MAGA Inc. against Gov. DeSantis for failure to constitute a legally sufficient complaint; no investigation was opened.

matters.title: Florida Commission on Ethics Complaint No. 23-059 (filed by Taylor Budowich): gifts from political committees and resign-to-run law
matters.summary: The Commission reviewed the complaint in executive session on 2023-04-21 for legal sufficiency only and dismissed it; no factual investigation preceded the review and the order states the conclusions do not reflect on the accuracy of the allegations. It found no allegation of an understanding that gifts would influence an official decision (s. 112.313(2)).

matters.title: Legislative audit of governor's office $19,029 lectern and road case purchase
matters.summary: Arkansas Legislative Audit released a report on the governor's office purchase, listing areas of potential noncompliance with state law (records, disposal procedures, a shredded bill of lading) and forwarding it to the Pulaski County prosecutor and the Attorney General. The governor's office said no laws were broken and called the report deeply flawed. No charges or further official action were found.

matters.title: Arkansas Legislative Audit report on governor's office lectern purchase
matters.summary: Auditors identified seven areas of potential noncompliance with state law by the governor's office relating to purchasing, state property and records in the purchase of a custom lectern; the report was sent to prosecuting attorneys. Attorney General Tim Griffin indicated he would not pursue charges, saying state purchasing laws do not apply to the governor. The governor's office called the report deeply flawed and said the state was reimbursed with private funds.
matters.authority: Arkansas Legislative Audit (Division of Legislative Audit)

matters.title: Phil Lyman challenge to Cox's place on the 2024 Republican primary ballot
matters.summary: Lyman alleged Cox did not gather the signatures needed for the 2024 primary ballot and asked the Utah Supreme Court to nullify the result. That court dismissed the petition, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear the appeal on 13 Jan 2025. Filing date approximate (August 2024).
matters.authority: Utah Supreme Court; U.S. Supreme Court

matters.title: Attorney General report on Lt. Gov. Reeves and Rankin County frontage road project
matters.summary: A 43-page report from then-Attorney General Jim Hood, a political rival in the 2019 governor's race, concluded that Reeves improperly sought to influence a road project near his neighborhood and impeded the investigation by withholding documents. Hood said he would not pursue charges. Reeves's campaign has disputed the report, according to coverage. The road was never built.
matters.penalty: None; the AG said he would not pursue charges, and no civil action was reported

matters.title: 1995 Nebraska DUI arrest; guilty plea to reckless driving
matters.summary: Arrested after a 1995 traffic stop in western Nebraska and booked at Dawes County Jail on a drunken-driving charge. On March 13, 1996 he pleaded guilty to a reduced charge of reckless driving, per the plea hearing transcript reported by the Associated Press. Pre-dates his public offices; he later acknowledged the facts during his 2018 campaign.
matters.penalty: $200 fine; 90-day license suspension

matters.title: House resolution to investigate impeachment of Gov. Walz fails in committee
matters.summary: A resolution alleging corrupt conduct in office relating to fraud in state programs was filed in January 2026. A motion to send it for investigation failed on an 8-8 tie vote in the Rules committee on April 15, 2026 (also reported by Fox 9 and KSTP). No impeachment articles advanced to a floor vote. Walz disputes the allegations; this is a legislative action, not a finding of misconduct.
matters.authority: Minnesota House Rules and Legislative Administration Committee

matters.title: Ethics complaints over role of First Spouse Aimee Kotek Wilson in governor's office
matters.summary: The commission split 4-4 on opening a formal investigation, short of the five votes needed, so the complaints were dismissed; the director had recommended dismissal after a preliminary review.

matters.title: Oregon Government Ethics Commission complaints over role of Governor's spouse
matters.summary: Two complaints alleged that Governor Kotek violated state ethics law by giving her wife, First Lady Aimee Kotek Wilson, office space and staff assistance. The commission's staff recommended dismissal. A motion to open a formal investigation deadlocked 4-4 and failed for lack of the five votes required, so the complaints were dismissed with no finding of a violation.

matters.title: Oregon House Conduct Committee workplace complaint filed by former Rep. Diego Hernandez
matters.summary: Former Rep. Diego Hernandez filed a legislative workplace complaint (filed 2021) over a May 2019 conversation with then-Speaker Kotek. An outside investigator found his account credible but concluded the conduct did not violate legislative workplace rules. On 31 Oct 2022 the House Conduct Committee split 2-2 on the hostile-workplace claim, dismissed the remaining claims unanimously, and the complaint ended with no finding of misconduct.

matters.title: BOLI investigation of sexual harassment in the Oregon Legislature: finding on legislative leadership
matters.summary: BOLI's January 2019 investigative report on harassment by former Sen. Jeff Kruse criticized legislative leadership. As reported by Willamette Week, BOLI found that Speaker Kotek and Senate President Courtney failed to take immediate and appropriate corrective action on unlawful employment practices based on sex. The commissioner's complaint was settled in March 2019. Kotek said as House Speaker she had no authority over a senator.
matters.authority: Oregon Bureau of Labor and Industries (BOLI)
matters.penalty: Legislature agreed to pay $1.322 million to resolve the commissioner's complaint (paid by the Legislature, not by Kotek personally)

matters.title: Wisconsin Elections Commission complaint Knudson v. Evers (Case EL 20-28) over signing the Certificate of Ascertainment
matters.summary: Commissioner Dean Knudson filed a sworn amended complaint naming Governor Evers as respondent, alleging a violation of Wis. Stat. 7.70(5) by signing and transmitting the Certificate of Ascertainment on November 30, 2020, before the recount deadlines had passed. The Commission found no probable cause of a violation of law or abuse of discretion and resolved the complaint.
matters.authority: Wisconsin Elections Commission (decision by special counsel DeWitt LLP)

matters.title: Hart-Scott-Rodino premerger notification violation (ICOS stock purchase)
matters.summary: The Justice Department sued and settled with Gates over buying more than $50 million of ICOS Corp. voting stock in 2002 without the advance antitrust filing required for large acquisitions; he agreed to pay a civil penalty.
matters.authority: U.S. Department of Justice (civil suit, U.S. District Court, Washington, D.C.)
matters.penalty: $800,000 civil penalty

matters.title: SEC v. Musk (2018): tweets about taking Tesla private
matters.summary: On Sept 27, 2018 the SEC filed a complaint in the S.D.N.Y. alleging securities fraud over Musk's Aug 7, 2018 tweets that he could take Tesla private at $420 per share with funding secured. Musk consented without admitting or denying the allegations; Final Judgment was entered Oct 16, 2018 and required, among other things, pre-approval of written communications that could contain information material to Tesla, with a $20 million penalty and a three-year bar on serving as Tesla chairman. In Feb 2019 the SEC moved for an order to show cause why Musk should not be held in contempt of the judgment, and in May 2023 the Second Circuit rejected Musk's challenge to the pre-approval requirement.
matters.authority: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission; U.S. District Court, S.D.N.Y.
matters.penalty: $20 million civil penalty (Musk) and $20 million (Tesla)

matters.title: SEC v. Musk (2025): late Twitter beneficial-ownership report
matters.summary: On Jan 14, 2025 the SEC sued Musk in D.D.C. alleging he filed late the Section 13(d) report of his Twitter stake in 2022. In May 2026 the SEC added the Elon Musk Revocable Trust as a defendant; the court entered a consent final judgment against the trust on July 8, 2026 (injunction and $1.5 million civil penalty, without admitting or denying), and on July 9, 2026 the SEC and Musk stipulated to dismissal of all claims against Musk personally with prejudice. The court's opinion stated it had significant misgivings but could not reject the settlement.
matters.authority: U.S. District Court, District of Columbia (SEC v. Musk, No. 1:25-cv-00105-SLS)
matters.penalty: $1.5 million civil penalty entered against the Elon Musk Revocable Trust; none against Musk personally

matters.title: SEC securities fraud charge over August 2018 'funding secured' tweet
matters.summary: The SEC charged Musk with securities fraud over his August 7, 2018 tweet about taking Tesla private at $420 per share; he settled without admitting or denying the allegations. Tesla separately paid $20 million.
matters.penalty: $20 million civil penalty; stepped down as Tesla chairman, barred from re-election as chairman for three years

matters.title: SEC suit over late disclosure of Twitter stake (Section 13(d))
matters.summary: The SEC alleged Musk took 11 days too long in March-April 2022 to disclose his 5% Twitter stake. A consent judgment was announced May 4, 2026 and approved by the court on July 8, 2026.
matters.authority: SEC; U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (Judge Sparkle Sooknanan)
matters.penalty: $1.5 million paid via a trust; injunction; SEC dropped disgorgement demand

matters.title: Structured Asset Sales v. Sheeran (Thinking Out Loud copyright suit), Second Circuit affirmance
matters.summary: Private copyright infringement suit over 'Thinking Out Loud' and Marvin Gaye's 'Let's Get It On'. Second Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Sheeran and co-defendants, finding no infringement.
matters.authority: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit

matters.title: Spain tax fraud case over image-rights income, 2011-2014
matters.summary: A Madrid state prosecutor accused Cristiano Ronaldo in June 2017 of four counts of tax fraud for 2011-2014, valued at EUR 14.7 million; he denied the accusation at a 31 July 2017 court hearing. Under a pre-agreed deal with the Spanish tax authorities, a Madrid court on 22 January 2019 accepted his guilty plea and a 23-month suspended prison sentence, with a total payment reported as EUR 18.8 million.
matters.authority: Spanish court, Madrid (Pozuelo de Alarcon investigating court and Madrid court)
matters.penalty: 23-month suspended prison sentence and fines reported as EUR 18.8 million in total

matters.title: Spanish tax fraud case (image-rights income), 2011-2014
matters.summary: Ronaldo accepted a plea agreement with Spanish prosecutors and was sentenced by a Madrid court for four tax offences relating to image-rights income; the prison term was not to be served.
matters.penalty: 23-month prison sentence (not served, as first offence under 2 years) and a EUR 18.8 million fine

matters.title: Mayorga v. Ronaldo (Las Vegas) civil suit dismissed; no criminal charges
matters.summary: Federal judge dismissed Kathryn Mayorga's civil suit with prejudice as a sanction for her attorney's bad-faith use of leaked documents, not on the merits. Clark County DA had declined criminal charges in 2019. Ronaldo has maintained the encounter was consensual.
matters.authority: U.S. District Court, District of Nevada (Judge Jennifer Dorsey); Clark County District Attorney

matters.title: Spain tax fraud case over image-rights income, 2007-2009
matters.summary: A state prosecutor filed a complaint on 12 June 2013 alleging tax fraud over image-rights income for 2007-2009. A Barcelona court convicted Lionel Messi and his father on 6 July 2016 of three counts and sentenced each to 21 months in prison plus a fine. Spain's Supreme Court rejected the appeal and upheld the sentence on 24 May 2017. In June 2017 the 21-month prison term was replaced with a fine reported as EUR 250,000.
matters.authority: Audiencia Provincial de Barcelona; Tribunal Supremo (Spain)
matters.penalty: 21-month prison sentence (replaced by a fine reported as EUR 250,000) plus a fine of about EUR 2 million

matters.title: Spanish Supreme Court upholds tax fraud conviction and 21-month sentence
matters.summary: Spain's Supreme Court rejected Messi's appeal and upheld his conviction for tax fraud over income from exploiting his image rights; his father's sentence was reduced from 21 to 15 months.
matters.penalty: 21-month prison sentence (upheld; reported as suspended under Spanish practice for sentences under two years) plus a fine; amount not stated on the fetched page

matters.title: Defaulted from 2020 US Open after ball struck a line judge
matters.summary: The tournament referee defaulted Djokovic from his fourth-round match after he hit a ball that struck a line judge, citing the Grand Slam rulebook. He apologised publicly.
matters.authority: United States Tennis Association / US Open tournament referee
matters.penalty: Default from the tournament, forfeiture of ranking points and $250,000 prize money, and a $10,000 fine

matters.title: MLB investigation into Ohtani over interpreter's illegal gambling closed; Ohtani deemed a victim of fraud
matters.summary: MLB opened a formal investigation in March 2024 after his interpreter Ippei Mizuhara was accused of gambling-related theft. MLB closed it in June 2024, treating Ohtani as a victim; Mizuhara was sentenced to 57 months in federal prison per a DOJ release (Ohtani named as victim).

matters.title: Reckless driving plea resolving May 2017 DUI arrest (Palm Beach County, Florida)
matters.summary: Woods pleaded guilty to reckless driving in Palm Beach County on 27 October 2017 under a plea agreement with prosecutors that settled the DUI charge from his May 2017 arrest; the plea carried no jail time.
matters.penalty: One year probation, $250 fine plus court costs, DUI school, 20 hours community service, drug testing; DUI charge dropped under a diversion program

matters.title: Presidential pardon for offenses related to his federal service
matters.summary: A full and unconditional pardon was granted covering any federal offenses from January 1, 2014 through the date of the pardon arising from his service as NIAID Director, member of the White House Coronavirus Task Force or COVID-19 Response Team, or Chief Medical Advisor to the President. The pardon is preemptive; no charges were filed against him.
matters.authority: President Joseph R. Biden Jr. (US Department of Justice, Office of the Pardon Attorney)

matters.title: Michael Black, MD v. Cable News Network, Inc. - summary judgment for Cooper
matters.summary: A surgeon sued CNN and several individuals, including Cooper, for defamation over a 2015 CNN report. The court granted Cooper's motion for summary judgment as to him; the case continued against other defendants.
matters.authority: Circuit Court, 15th Judicial Circuit, Palm Beach County, Florida

matters.title: United States v. Stewart: ImClone-related obstruction and false-statement conviction
matters.summary: A federal jury in the S.D.N.Y. found Stewart guilty on four counts on March 5, 2004; she was sentenced on July 16, 2004 to five months in prison, five months of home confinement and a $30,000 fine. The Second Circuit upheld the conviction in January 2006; she completed the sentence in 2005.
matters.authority: U.S. District Court, S.D.N.Y. (Judge Miriam Goldman Cedarbaum); U.S. Court of Appeals, Second Circuit
matters.penalty: Five months in prison, five months home confinement, $30,000 fine

matters.title: SEC v. Stewart and Bacanovic: ImClone stock sale
matters.summary: On June 4, 2003 the SEC filed a civil complaint in the S.D.N.Y. alleging insider trading and obstruction concerning Stewart's December 2001 sale of ImClone stock. On Aug 7, 2006 Stewart consented, without admitting or denying the allegations, to a permanent injunction, disgorgement with interest, a civil penalty and a five-year bar from serving as a director of a public company.
matters.authority: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission; U.S. District Court, S.D.N.Y. (03 Civ. 4070)
matters.penalty: $137,019 civil penalty; $58,062 disgorgement and prejudgment interest; five-year director bar

matters.title: SEC v. Martha Stewart and Peter Bacanovic (ImClone insider trading)
matters.summary: The SEC sued Stewart in June 2003 over her December 2001 ImClone stock sales. In August 2006 she consented to final judgment without admitting or denying the allegations.
matters.authority: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission / U.S. District Court, S.D.N.Y.
matters.penalty: $58,062 disgorgement and prejudgment interest, $137,019 civil penalty; five-year bar from serving as a public-company director and five-year limit on officer/employee roles

matters.title: United States v. Martha Stewart (ImClone-related obstruction case)
matters.summary: A jury convicted Stewart on 5 March 2004 of conspiracy, obstruction and false statements to federal investigators; a securities fraud charge was dismissed before verdict. She served her sentence and was released in 2005.
matters.authority: U.S. District Court (New York); appeal to U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
matters.penalty: Five months in prison and five months of home detention (July 2004 sentence)

matters.title: Mzamane v. Winfrey defamation suit (E.D. Pa.) settled before trial
matters.summary: A former headmistress of Winfrey's South African girls' school sued her for defamation; the judge had earlier declined to dismiss the case. The parties settled shortly before the scheduled trial, on undisclosed terms.
matters.authority: U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia)
matters.penalty: Terms not disclosed

matters.title: Herring Networks (OAN) v. Maddow defamation suit dismissed; affirmed by Ninth Circuit
matters.summary: Herring Networks sued Maddow and her employers for $10 million over a 2019 segment. The district court dismissed the suit with prejudice and the Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding the statement was protected speech.
matters.authority: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit; U.S. District Court, S.D. Cal.
matters.penalty: Plaintiff ordered to pay more than $250,000 in Maddow's legal fees

matters.title: Fox shareholder derivative suit over workplace harassment oversight settled
matters.summary: A shareholder derivative suit in the Delaware Court of Chancery (City of Monroe Employees' Retirement System v. Murdoch, No. 2017-0833) named Fox officers and directors including Rupert Murdoch over the company's handling of sexual harassment at Fox News. A $90 million settlement, paid by insurers to the company, was announced on 20 November 2017 with governance reforms; the defendants did not admit wrongdoing. Court approval was reported on 9 February 2018.
matters.penalty: $90 million paid by insurers to the company; governance reforms

matters.title: Fine for disobeying police order, Malmo oil-port protest (June 2023)
matters.summary: Convicted of failing to obey a police order to leave a protest blocking oil trucks at Malmo harbour on 19 June 2023; she admitted the act but argued necessity.
matters.penalty: 1,500 SEK fine plus 1,000 SEK to the crime victims fund

matters.title: Fine for disobeying police order, Malmo oil terminal protest (July 2023)
matters.summary: Fined for taking part in a 24 July 2023 protest at an oil terminal in Malmo and not leaving when ordered by police.
matters.penalty: 2,250 SEK fine (as reported by AP)

matters.title: Fine for disobeying police, Swedish parliament blockade (March 2024)
matters.summary: Convicted on two counts of civil disobedience after refusing to leave the parliament main entrance when police ordered her to on 12 and 14 March 2024; she denied the charges.
matters.penalty: 6,000 SEK fine plus 1,000 SEK damages and interest

matters.title: Public Order Act charge, London oil conference protest
matters.summary: Charged under section 14 of the Public Order Act 1986 after an October 2023 protest outside an oil and gas conference; the district judge found the police conditions unlawfully unclear and found all five defendants not guilty.

matters.title: Rivonia Trial: sabotage conviction and life sentence
matters.summary: Mandela and seven co-accused were found guilty of sabotage in the Rivonia Trial (verdict 11 June 1964) and sentenced to life imprisonment on 12 June 1964.
matters.authority: Supreme Court of South Africa (Palace of Justice, Pretoria)
matters.penalty: Life imprisonment

matters.title: FEC MUR 8145: complaint over $500,000 contribution to Democratic Party of Oregon
matters.summary: A complaint by Jeffrey T. Eager alleged that Sen. Wyden and consultant Diana Rogalle solicited or directed an excessive contribution in connection with a nonfederal election. The Commission voted 4-0 to dismiss the allegation and close the file.

matters.title: FEC MUR 8145: Ronald Wyden
matters.summary: The Federal Election Commission's Matter Under Review 8145 ("Ronald Wyden") named Ron Wyden as a respondent; the Commission's disposition for that respondent was "Dismissed-Other".

matters.title: Judicial Watch Senate ethics complaint over wife's consulting work and his legislative activity
matters.summary: Judicial Watch asked the Senate Ethics Committee to investigate Sen. Whitehouse over his wife's consulting work for environmental groups. The Committee dismissed the complaint by letter dated Aug. 16, 2024, concluding his actions did not violate federal law, Senate rules or other standards of conduct and that it intended no further action.
matters.authority: U.S. Senate Select Committee on Ethics

matters.title: FEC MUR 7893: William B. Wachtel
matters.summary: The Federal Election Commission's Matter Under Review 7893 ("William B. Wachtel") named Sheldon Whitehouse as a respondent; the Commission's disposition for that respondent was "No Reason to Believe".

matters.title: SEC failure-to-supervise settlement
matters.summary: The SEC found failures to supervise former portfolio manager Mathew Martoma and settled the proceeding. Cohen consented without admitting or denying the findings. The restriction concerned supervisory activity and expired under the settlement terms; it is not a criminal insider-trading conviction.
matters.penalty: Prohibited from supervising funds managing outside money until 2018; independent consultant, compliance reviews and SEC examinations.

phases.label: President, 1861-1865
phases.summary: Led the Union through the Civil War, issued the Emancipation Proclamation, and secured congressional passage of the Thirteenth Amendment, while suspending habeas corpus and approving the Dakota executions.

social.basis: The Emancipation Proclamation recognized the freedom of about 3.5 million enslaved people and the Thirteenth Amendment (House 119-56) abolished slavery; offset by suspension of habeas corpus, the draft and the approval of 38 Dakota executions.

economic.basis: Homestead Act (160 acres), Morrill Land-Grant Act, Pacific Railway Acts, national banking acts, greenbacks (about $450 million circulating) and income tax (about one-fifth of revenue) built long-run institutions; national debt rose from $65 million (1860) to $2 billion (1866) in wartime.

position.basis: Sixteenth president and commander in chief; won 39.8% and 180 electoral votes in 1860 and about 55% and 212 of 233 electoral votes in 1864.

education.basis: Under 12 months of formal schooling by age 15, self-taught; read law on his own and was admitted to the Illinois bar on September 9, 1836.

phases.label: President, two terms
phases.summary: Vetoed the Second Bank's recharter, paid off the national debt in 1835, signed Indian removal and was censured by the Senate in 1834.

social.basis: Signed the Indian Removal Act of 1830 (House 102-97); the Treaty of New Echota was ratified in 1836 and removal killed as many as 4,000 of 18,000 Cherokee in 1838; Jackson reportedly said of Worcester v. Georgia that Marshall 'has made his decision, now let him enforce it' (disputed). Judgement-heavy.

economic.basis: Paid off the entire national debt in January 1835 (the only time in U.S. history); vetoed the Bank recharter (July 10, 1832); land sales rose from 2M acres in 1829 to 12.5M in 1835 and the Panic of 1837 depression lasted until 1841.

position.basis: President of the United States, 1829-1837.

education.basis: Tutored by a local minister as a boy; no college. Studied law under Spruce Macay and John Stokes from 1784 and was admitted to the North Carolina bar in 1787.

misconduct.basis: On March 28, 1834 the Senate voted 26-20 to censure him for assuming authority not granted by the Constitution in removing federal deposits from the Second Bank; expunged on January 16-17, 1837.

phases.label: President, 1865-1869
phases.summary: Succeeded Lincoln, opposed congressional Reconstruction and the Fourteenth Amendment, had ten vetoes overridden, and was impeached in 1868 and acquitted by one vote.

social.basis: Vetoed the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and the Freedmen's Bureau bills (ten vetoes overridden), opposed the Fourteenth Amendment, and declined to intervene as Southern states passed Black Codes; Memphis and New Orleans riots against Black residents occurred under his policy. Historians rank him among the worst presidents.

economic.basis: Alaska purchase (1867) and an end to postwar currency contraction in January 1868 with minimal inflation, but the national debt stood at $2.8 billion and the Southern Homestead Act yielded few patents for freedpeople; no growth figures, judged mixed.

position.basis: Seventeenth president of the United States, April 1865 to March 1869.

education.basis: Never attended school; apprenticed to a tailor at about age ten and taught basic literacy by co-workers and his wife.

misconduct.basis: The House impeached him on February 24, 1868 (126-47) over the Tenure of Office Act; the Senate voted 35-19 on three articles, one short of the 36 needed, and acquitted him. Resolved in his favour.

phases.label: Early career
phases.summary: Obama graduated from Columbia (1983), worked as a Chicago community organizer (1985-1988), earned a Harvard law degree (1991), practised and taught law, served in the Illinois Senate (1997-2004) and won the 2004 U.S. Senate election.

wealth.basis: The Obamas' 2004 joint income was $207,342 per CBS News' summary of the returns they released (2000-2003 range: $176,965-$238,327). The Census Bureau's Table H-1 puts the lower limit of the top 5% of U.S. households in 2004 at about $157,200 (www2.census.gov historical-income-households h01ar.xlsx), so income sat in the top 5% but below the top 1%. No net-worth figure was found for the phase.

position.basis: Illinois state senator for the 13th district from January 1997 to November 2004 (a legislator's role); earlier roles were community organizer and civil-rights attorney, and he was the 2004 U.S. Senate nominee and winner.

education.basis: Holds a J.D. from Harvard Law School (1991, magna cum laude) after a B.A. from Columbia University (1983); no doctorate.

phases.label: President, first term
phases.summary: First term as 44th President of the United States, 20 January 2009 to 20 January 2013, covering the Recovery Act, the Affordable Care Act and Dodd-Frank.

health.basis: Physician to the President's October 2011 exam (second periodic exam) reported 'excellent health' and 'fit for duty', tobacco free, total cholesterol 193 mg/dL ('ideal'), blood pressure 107/71, no conditions reported. The February 2010 exam had advised continued smoking-cessation efforts and borderline-high LDL (138), a minor documented concern. Minor documented items place it at 4.

social.basis: The ACA dependent-coverage provision (effective Sept 2010) raised insurance among adults 19-25 from 64% to 73% (Sept 2010-June 2011, NHIS), about 2.5 million people, per an HHS/ASPE brief on NCHS data; it is an administration analysis, and a peer-reviewed study (Sommers et al.) found the gain partly offset by fewer young adults insured in their own names. The law's main coverage expansions took effect in 2014 (second term). Other first-term measures were not evaluated here. Scored 3: one provision evaluated, source is an administration brief.

wealth.basis: Adjusted gross income on released joint returns: 2009 $5,505,409; 2010 $1,728,096; 2011 $789,674; 2012 $608,611. IRS-based top-1% AGI cutoffs (Tax Foundation, Table 7): $351,968 (2009), $369,691 (2010), $388,905 (2011), $434,682 (2012), so each year exceeded the top-1% threshold. A top-0.1% threshold was not sourced, so 5 is not scored.

economic.basis: CBO estimated the Recovery Act raised real GDP by 1.1-3.1% and employment by 1.2-3.3 million in early 2011, with effects peaking in the first half of 2010 and diminishing after, at a total cost of about $830 billion; its 2010 analysis found a slight long-run output reduction. 67.5% of IGM panelists agreed benefits would exceed costs (July 2014 poll). GAO found Dodd-Frank's effect on bank funding advantages inconclusive. Overall: mostly favourable short-run evidence with a fiscal cost; effects debated.

position.basis: Head of state and government of the United States (President), inaugurated 20 January 2009.

standing.basis: Gallup's Obama term-averages report puts his first-term average job approval at 49.1% (overall 2009-2017 average 47.9%), within the 35-50% band.

education.basis: Holds a J.D. from Harvard Law School (1991) and a B.A. from Columbia University (1983); no doctorate.

phases.label: President, second term
phases.summary: Second term as President, 20 January 2013 to 20 January 2017, covering implementation of the Affordable Care Act's coverage expansions and post-recession recovery.

health.basis: The June 2014 memo from the Physician to the President (exam in May 2014) states 'overall health is excellent'. Minor documented items: recurrent right plantar fasciitis, mild vitamin D deficiency treated with daily vitamin D, occasional nicotine gum, LDL 137 mg/dL, several benign skin tags. No significant past medical history. The 2016 exam report was not retrieved.

social.basis: CDC/NCHS: uninsured persons of all ages fell from 16.0% (48.6M) in 2010 to 9.0% (28.6M) in 2016; adults 18-64 in expansion states fell from 18.4% (2013) to 9.2% (2016) vs 22.7% to 17.9% in non-expansion states. Miller, Johnson and Wherry (QJE 2021, NBER w26081) found Medicaid expansion cut near-elderly adult mortality 9.4%. Contested: the Oregon experiment found no significant change in measured BP, cholesterol or glucose; premiums and attribution are debated.

wealth.basis: Adjusted gross income: 2013 $481,098; 2014 $477,383; 2015 $436,065 (White House releases; 2016 return not found). IRS-based top-1% AGI cutoffs (Tax Foundation): $428,713 (2013), $465,626 (2014), $480,930 (2015); top-5% cutoffs $179,760-$195,778. Income was above the top-1% line in 2013-2014 and just under it in 2015, so between the top 5% and top 1%. No net-worth figure sourced.

economic.basis: In the IGM panel on the ACA, about 70% agreed the health and well-being gains for the newly insured exceed the costs, while 52% said the subsidies would not reduce total health-care spending. CBO reported the federal deficit at $587 billion in 2016 (3.2% of GDP incl. timing shifts), down from 9.9% in FY2009, while debt held by the public reached about 77% of GDP. Efficiency, labour-supply and fiscal-sustainability effects were debated; evidence mixed.

position.basis: Head of state and government of the United States; re-elected in 2012 and served until 20 January 2017.

standing.basis: Gallup's Obama term-averages report puts his second-term average job approval at 46.7% (first term 49.1%, overall 47.9%), within the 35-50% band.

education.basis: Holds a J.D. from Harvard Law School (1991) and a B.A. from Columbia University (1983); no doctorate.

misconduct.basis: 2 documented matter(s) in the reviewed legal record, counted as the misconduct meter counts them.

phases.label: Civil War officer, Indiana lawyer and US Senator
phases.summary: Colonel of the 70th Indiana, brevet brigadier general, Supreme Court reporter and Senator from Indiana 1881-1887.

position.basis: US Senator from Indiana, 4 March 1881 - 3 March 1887.

education.basis: Graduated Miami University 1852, then read law under Judge Bellamy Storer and was admitted to the Ohio bar in 1854.

phases.label: President of the United States
phases.summary: The 'Billion-Dollar Congress': Sherman Antitrust and Silver Purchase Acts, McKinley Tariff, expanded pensions and forest reserves, followed by heavy 1890 midterm losses.

social.basis: Dependent and Disability Pension Act expanded veterans' pensions ($135M), about 22 million acres of forest reserves created and six western states admitted, but the Federal Elections (Lodge) Bill to protect Black voting was tabled 35-34 in the Senate in 1891.

economic.basis: McKinley Tariff set the highest average tariff in US history; Sherman Silver Purchase Act (4.5M oz a month) accelerated gold depletion; spending hit $1B and the Treasury surplus was gone by 1892, ahead of the Panic of 1893.

position.basis: Head of state and government 4 March 1889 - 4 March 1893.

phases.label: President, 1993-2001
phases.summary: Presided over the longest peacetime expansion and federal budget surpluses, signed welfare reform and CHIP, and was impeached in 1998 and acquitted in 1999.

social.basis: FMLA (12 weeks unpaid leave), CHIP (1997), child tax credit and minimum wage rise to $5.15 for about 10 million workers; PRWORA cut cash assistance recipients from 12.2 million (1996) to 5.3 million (2001), with contested effects on hardship. Crime bill and Brady Act not assessed.

economic.basis: Deficit fell from $255.1 billion (FY1993) to surpluses of $69.3 billion (1998) through $236.2 billion (2000), debt fell from 47.9% to 31.5% of GDP, unemployment about 4% by 2000, poverty rate 11.3%; median household income rose from $38,262 (1995) to $42,151 (2000, 2000 dollars). Income inequality grew.

position.basis: 42nd president, elected 1992 and re-elected 1996.

standing.basis: Gallup average job approval of 55% (range 37-73%); final Gallup reading 66%, the highest of any departing president since World War II.

education.basis: Georgetown B.A. (1968), Rhodes scholar at Oxford without degree, Yale Law School J.D. (1973).

misconduct.basis: Impeached by the House December 19, 1998 (perjury 228-206, obstruction 221-212) and acquitted by the Senate February 12, 1999 (45-55 and 50-50); a federal court civil contempt ruling and bar referral; Arkansas law licence suspended five years on January 19, 2001 and suspended from practising before the Supreme Court. Whitewater probes found insufficient evidence to charge him.

phases.label: Massachusetts legislator, Lieutenant Governor and Governor
phases.summary: Rose from the Massachusetts House to governor; the 1919 Boston police strike made him nationally known.

position.basis: 48th Governor of Massachusetts, 2 January 1919 - 6 January 1921, after serving as President of the state Senate and Lieutenant Governor.

education.basis: AB cum laude, Amherst College; read law and was admitted to the bar.

phases.label: President of the United States
phases.summary: Tax cuts and debt reduction during the Roaring Twenties, restrictive immigration quotas, farm-aid vetoes and the Harding scandal clean-up.

social.basis: Indian Citizenship Act 1924 (about two-thirds already citizens) and the Flood Control Act of 1928, but the Immigration Act of 1924 cut quotas to 2% of the 1890 population, he abandoned anti-lynching efforts, did not denounce the Klan and initially refused flood aid in 1927.

economic.basis: Top income tax rate cut from 71% to 46% by 1924, about a quarter of the $22.3B debt retired, GDP rose from $85.2B (1924) to $101.4B (1929), low unemployment; vetoed McNary-Haugen farm bills in 1927 and 1928.

position.basis: Head of state and government 2 August 1923 - 4 March 1929.

phases.label: Collector of the Port of New York
phases.summary: Ran the New York Custom House under Grant until President Hayes removed him in July 1878 after a commission found it overstaffed.

position.basis: Appointed Collector of the Port of New York by Grant in December 1871 and served until July 11, 1878, heading the New York Custom House (income over $50,000 in some years under the moiety system, $12,000 salary after 1874); a senior executive post below cabinet level.

education.basis: Graduated from Union College in 1848 (Phi Beta Kappa) and was admitted to the New York bar in 1854.

phases.label: President, from Garfield's death
phases.summary: Signed the Pendleton Civil Service Act and the Chinese Exclusion Act and began rebuilding the Navy while concealing Bright's disease.

health.basis: Diagnosed with Bright's disease (kidney ailment) shortly after taking office; he tried to keep it private and poor health limited his effort for the 1884 nomination.

social.basis: Signed the Chinese Exclusion Act (May 6, 1882; 10-year ban; about 250,000 Chinese immigrants then lived in the U.S.) and the Edmunds Act on polygamy, but also the Pendleton Civil Service Act (January 16, 1883). Judgement-heavy.

economic.basis: Pendleton Act covered about 10% of federal jobs; the surplus reached $145M by 1882 and the Tariff of 1883 (average cut 1.47%) 'had no effect on the budget surplus'; Rivers and Harbors bill ($19M) vetoed and the veto overridden.

position.basis: President of the United States, September 19, 1881 to March 1885.

education.basis: Graduated from Union College in 1848 and was admitted to the New York bar in 1854.

misconduct.basis: 1 documented matter(s) in the reviewed legal record, counted as the misconduct meter counts them.

phases.label: Early career
phases.summary: Trump graduated from Wharton in 1968, became president of his father's real-estate company in 1971 and developed Manhattan and Atlantic City properties.

position.basis: President of his father's real-estate company from 1971 (renamed the Trump Organization), which developed the Grand Hyatt (1980) and Atlantic City casinos (Trump Plaza, bought out of Holiday Corp. for $70 million in 1986; Trump's Castle, 1985). The score rests on asset scale; no employee count was found for the mid-1980s, and he started in the family firm in the late 1960s.

education.basis: Bachelor of Science in economics, Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, May 1968 (after starting at Fordham University in 1964). No graduate degree.

phases.label: President, first term
phases.summary: Trump served as 45th President of the United States from 20 January 2017 to 20 January 2021.

health.basis: White House physician memos (Feb 2019: 'very good health overall'; 243 lb at 6'3", BMI about 30 by calculation; rosuvastatin raised to 40 mg for high cholesterol). In October 2020 he was treated for COVID-19 at Walter Reed with remdesivir and was off supplemental oxygen within days (3 Oct 2020 memo).

social.basis: Evidence is divided. CBO/JCT projected the 2017 individual-mandate repeal would raise the uninsured by 13 million by 2027 (4 million in 2019), with a caveat that revised methods would probably give smaller numbers; the Lancet Commission on Trump-era policy attributed large avoidable health losses to rollbacks and the COVID-19 response, estimates other analysts contest. DOJ's First Step Act reports show lower recidivism among released people (15.9% vs about 43%), though selection effects limit causal reading.

wealth.basis: Forbes estimated $3.1 billion (rank 248, 2017) and $2.5 billion (rank 339, 2020, down from $3.1 billion in 2019), all on the Forbes 400. Saez-Zucman (BPEA, Fall 2019, Table 2) put the top 0.1% family wealth threshold at about $28-41 million in 2019 dollars, so his net worth was far above it.

economic.basis: CBO estimated the 2017 tax act (Pub. L. 115-97) raises real GDP about 0.7% on average over 2018-2028 and adds about $1.9 trillion to deficits; in an IGM panel only 1 of 42 economists agreed it would make GDP substantially higher in ten years while 88% expected a higher debt ratio. Fajgelbaum et al. (QJE 2020) put the 2018-19 tariffs' net aggregate real income loss at $7.2 billion (0.04% of GDP).

position.basis: 45th President of the United States, head of state and government, 20 January 2017 to 20 January 2021.

standing.basis: Gallup job approval averaged 41.1% over 2017-2021 (range 34%-49%, final reading 34% in January 2021), the lowest term average in Gallup's series. The 35-50% band applies.

education.basis: Bachelor of Science in economics, Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, 1968; no graduate degree.

misconduct.basis: Two findings with resolution dates in the term: Trump University $25 million class and NY AG settlement (final approval 31 Mar 2017, no admission) and the Trump Foundation order (7 Nov 2019, $2 million; he admitted misusing Foundation funds). First impeachment acquitted 5 Feb 2020 (resolved in his favour); second impeachment and the 2019 Carroll defamation suit were open at term end. The matters file may be incomplete for this era.

phases.label: President, second term
phases.summary: Trump has served as 47th President of the United States since 20 January 2025, the term being ongoing.

health.basis: White House physician memos: April 2025 exam 'excellent cognitive and physical health' (MoCA 30/30; two cholesterol medications, aspirin); July 2025 chronic venous insufficiency, described as benign, no DVT or arterial disease; May 2026 annual exam (238 lb, 75 in). A treated chronic condition, otherwise normal findings.

social.basis: CBO estimates Pub. L. 119-21's Medicaid provisions raise the uninsured by 7.5 million in 2034 and its SNAP provisions cut participation by about 2.4 million in an average month; the Lancet (2025) projected 14 million additional deaths by 2030 from USAID cuts, a model result critics dispute. Mostly projections.

wealth.basis: Forbes real-time estimate $6.9 billion on 10 Oct 2026 (Forbes had $5.1 billion in March 2025 and $4.3 billion on the 2024 Forbes 400). Saez-Zucman (BPEA, Fall 2019, Table 2) put the top 0.1% family wealth threshold at about $28-41 million in 2019 dollars.

economic.basis: CBO/JCT: Pub. L. 119-21 adds $3.4 trillion to deficits over 2025-2034 with real GDP about 0.5% higher; distribution favours the top decile. Yale Budget Lab: the 2025 tariffs raise prices 1.2% and shrink long-run GDP 0.3%; IGM panels on tariffs saw consumer-borne costs. The Supreme Court held the IEEPA tariffs unlawful on 20 Feb 2026 (CBO: $2.0 trillion deficit effect before refunds).

position.basis: 47th President of the United States, head of state and government, from 20 January 2025.

standing.basis: Gallup readings fell from 47% (Feb 2025) to 41% (Oct 2025) and 36% (Nov and Dec 2025); Gallup stopped the series in 2026. Pew measured 34% in July 2026 and 30% in Oct 2026. The phase average is near the bottom of the 35-50% band; later readings are below it.

education.basis: Bachelor of Science in economics, Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, 1968; no graduate degree.

misconduct.basis: Two findings resolved in the term: Carroll (2022 action) $5 million verdict final when certiorari was denied 29 Jun 2026 and rehearing 17 Aug 2026; Trump v. Clinton sanctions (about $938,000) affirmed by the Eleventh Circuit 26 Nov 2025. Open: NY AG civil fraud (Court of Appeals), Carroll 2019 action (cert. pending), hush-money appeal. Favourable: Fulton County dismissal 26 Nov 2025. Counting the open liability matters as findings would give 5.

phases.label: President, 1953-1961
phases.summary: Ended the Korean War, launched the Interstate Highway System and NASA, enforced school desegregation at Little Rock, and governed through three mild recessions with serious health events in 1955-57.

health.basis: Serious heart attack September 24, 1955; surgery June 9, 1956 for a bowel obstruction linked to Crohn's disease; mild stroke November 25, 1957; seven heart attacks in total before death in 1969.

social.basis: Federalized the Arkansas Guard and sent the 101st Airborne to Little Rock (1957); Civil Rights Acts of 1957 and 1960 were weak (6.4% of Southern Black students in integrated schools by 1960); expanded Social Security to millions and signed the National Defense Education Act.

economic.basis: Inflation kept near zero, federal debt fell from 57.2% to 43.6% of GDP, personal income rose 45% and the Interstate system was authorized; but there were three recessions (1953-54, 1957-58, 1960-61) and deficits in five of eight budgets.

position.basis: 34th president and commander in chief, elected in 1952 and 1956.

standing.basis: Gallup average approval of about 65% (range 48-79%) per the Gallup table; the biography article gives 63%. Below 50% only briefly in 1958 and 1960.

education.basis: Graduated from West Point in the middle of the class of 1915, then first of 245 at the Command and General Staff College (1926).

phases.label: President, New Deal years 1933-1941
phases.summary: Responded to the Depression with banking reform, the Social Security and Wagner Acts and relief programmes; the court-packing plan was defeated and a recession struck in 1937-38.

health.basis: Paralysed from the waist down by polio (or Guillain-Barre) since August 1921, a documented permanent disability managed throughout the term; no cardiac disease documented until 1944.

social.basis: Social Security Act created old-age pensions, unemployment insurance and ADC (excluding agricultural and domestic workers); Wagner Act raised union membership from 3 million to 8 million; deposit insurance protected savers. Limits: exclusions weakened coverage for Black workers.

economic.basis: GNP was 34% higher in 1936 than in 1932 and 58% higher in 1940; Glass-Steagall/FDIC cut bank failures to near zero and the SEC restored disclosure; but unemployment was still about 20% in 1935 and the economy recontracted in 1937-38.

position.basis: President of the United States, elected four times; re-elected in 1936 in one of the largest landslides in American history.

standing.basis: Gallup average job approval of 63% across the presidency (range 48-83%); phase-specific series not available, so the whole-presidency average is used.

education.basis: Harvard A.B. in history (1903); attended Columbia Law School 1904-1907 and left after passing the bar without a law degree.

phases.label: Wartime president, 1941-1945
phases.summary: Mobilized the economy for World War II, created the FEPC and signed the GI Bill, ordered the internment of about 120,000 Japanese Americans, and died in office after documented heart failure.

health.basis: March 1944 tests at Bethesda found hypertension, atherosclerosis, coronary artery disease with angina and congestive heart failure; his physician publicly denied he was in poor health during the 1944 campaign. Died April 12, 1945 of a massive intracerebral hemorrhage.

social.basis: FEPC was the first national programme against employment discrimination and the GI Bill was passed, but the administration relocated and interned approximately 120,000 Japanese Americans. Mixed.

economic.basis: GNP grew 56% from 1940 to 1945; unemployment fell from 7.7 million (spring 1940) to 1.5 million (fall 1942); Revenue Act of 1942 created withholding and expanded income-taxpayers from about 4 million to over 40 million. Wartime deficits and top rates of 94% noted.

position.basis: Commander in chief and head of state during World War II; elected to a fourth term in 1944.

standing.basis: Gallup average job approval of 63% across the presidency (range 48-83%); phase-specific series not available.

education.basis: Harvard A.B. in history (1903); left Columbia Law School in 1907 after passing the bar, without a law degree.

phases.label: President, one term
phases.summary: Backed the Kansas-Nebraska Act, bought the Gadsden strip and lost renomination in 1856 amid Bleeding Kansas.

health.basis: Described as 'a heavy drinker for much of his life' (died of cirrhosis in 1869); he and his wife suffered severe depression after their son's death in January 1853, which likely affected his performance as president.

social.basis: His backing of the Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) nullified the Missouri Compromise and led to a 'long and violent conflict' over slavery's expansion; the Ostend Manifesto proposed taking Cuba. Judgement-heavy.

position.basis: President of the United States, 1853-1857.

education.basis: Graduated fifth in a class of 14 at Bowdoin College in 1824, read law, studied at Northampton Law School and was admitted to the New Hampshire bar in late 1827.

phases.label: Vice President of the United States
phases.summary: Two terms under Reagan, during which the Iran-Contra affair raised questions about his knowledge of arms-for-hostages dealings.

position.basis: Vice President 1981-1989 (second office, no executive authority of its own).

education.basis: BA in economics, Yale 1948, Phi Beta Kappa.

misconduct.basis: Never charged in Iran-Contra; biographer Meacham notes no evidence he knew of the diversion to the Contras. Independent counsel Walsh nevertheless wrote of a pattern of 'deception and obstruction' involving senior officials and Bush after the 1992 pardons. Scored as a matter not resolved by any finding against him.

phases.label: President of the United States
phases.summary: Gulf War victory and record approval in early 1991, the ADA and Clean Air Act amendments, then recession, a broken tax pledge and defeat in 1992.

health.basis: Graves' disease disclosed in May 1991 (treated, thyroid condition); no incapacity documented in office.

social.basis: Americans with Disabilities Act (1990), Clean Air Act Amendments (1990, aimed at acid rain and smog), Civil Rights Act of 1991 and Oil Pollution Act of 1990 signed; unemployment hardship in 1990-92 offsets part of the gain.

economic.basis: Mild recession from 1990; unemployment rose from 5.9% (1989) to 7.8% (mid-1991); deficit grew from $152.6B (FY1989) to $290.3B (FY1992); S&L cleanup cost over $100B; OBRA-90 (October 1990) later credited with groundwork for 1990s surpluses.

position.basis: Head of state and government 20 January 1989 - 20 January 1993.

standing.basis: Gallup job approval peaked at 89% (March 1991, highest in Gallup history), fell below 50% by January 1992 and was 56% at exit; Gallup-reported term average about 61% and low 29% (July 1992) per Gallup summary.

misconduct.basis: Iran-Contra: never charged; on 24 December 1992 he pardoned six officials including Weinberger, which Walsh called a completed cover-up. No court or ethics-body finding against Bush himself.

phases.label: Former President
phases.summary: Post-presidency in Houston, with advancing vascular parkinsonism in later years.

health.basis: Hip replacements in 2000 and 2007; leg weakness from vascular parkinsonism, wheelchair from 2011; died 30 November 2018 aged 94.

standing.basis: Gallup term-average job approval 60.9% (highest 89% Feb 1991, lowest 29% Jul 1992); 50-65% band.

misconduct.basis: 1 documented matter(s) in the reviewed legal record, counted as the misconduct meter counts them.

phases.label: Business and governor
phases.summary: Bush worked in oil exploration, was managing general partner of the Texas Rangers baseball club from 1989 and sold his stake in 1998, and served as Texas governor from January 1995 to December 2000.

health.basis: The 2001 White House medical summary records benign colonic adenomatous polyps removed at screening in July 1998 and Dec 1999, a 1997 knee meniscal repair, mild hearing loss, no hypertension, diabetes or heart disease, and a June 2000 Cooper Clinic treadmill of 24 minutes. Minor, treated findings only.

wealth.basis: Tax year 2000 taxable income was $744,682 (White House release); CNN (Apr 2000) reported 1998 income of about $18.4M after the Rangers sale. IRS SOI Bulletin Winter 2010 Table 5: top 1% AGI floor $313,469 in 2000; top 0.1% floor $1,324,487 in 2001. Typical-year income sits in the top 1%; 1998 exceeded the top 0.1% floor. Net worth not scored.

position.basis: Highest role in the phase: Governor of Texas (Jan 17, 1995 to Dec 21, 2000, re-elected 1998), a statewide office. He was also managing general partner of the Texas Rangers from 1989.

education.basis: Yale University BA in history (1968) and Harvard Business School MBA (1975), so a professional/master's degree was held from 1975.

misconduct.basis: One finding in the site's reviewed list: a 1976 Maine operating-under-the-influence charge, to which Mr. Bush pleaded guilty (fine $150, temporary suspension of Maine driving privileges); it became public in 2000. No other reviewed matter is dated in this phase.

phases.label: President, first term
phases.summary: Bush served as 43rd President from January 20, 2001, to January 20, 2005, a term that included the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts, No Child Left Behind, the PEPFAR launch, the Medicare drug benefit law and the Iraq invasion.

health.basis: Physician summaries (2001 on) rated him fit for duty. Dec 2004 exam: mild coronary artery calcification in a low-to-very-low risk category with daily aspirin and a statin advised, a shoulder lesion biopsied and facial lesions to be frozen; earlier mild hearing loss and benign polyps. Preventive treatment, no serious or incapacitating condition.

social.basis: Evidence is divided across signature policies. Dee and Jacob (NBER 15531) found NCLB raised 4th and 8th grade math scores and no reading gain. PEPFAR was associated with lower adult mortality (OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.72-0.99; Hein et al. 2020 replication, disputed by an earlier study). The Iraq Family Health Survey (NEJM 2008, via WHO) estimated 151,000 violent deaths Mar 2003-Jun 2006 (range 104,000-223,000).

wealth.basis: Adjusted gross income was $856,056 (2002) and $822,126 (2003) per White House-released returns reported by NBC. IRS SOI Bulletin Winter 2010 Table 5 AGI floors: top 1% $285,424 (2002) and $295,495 (2003); top 0.1% $1,191,673 and $1,262,760. Income was above the top-1% floor and below the top-0.1% floor.

economic.basis: Gale and Potter (Brookings, 2002) concluded the 2001 tax cut would reduce the future economy's size, raise interest rates and be fiscally unsustainable as written; others stress incentive effects, so the growth sign is disputed. CRS: tax cuts were about half of the legislative shift from the $128B FY2001 surplus to deficits; Part D adds an unfunded entitlement. Evidence leans fiscally negative, growth contested.

position.basis: Head of state and government as President of the United States, January 20, 2001 to January 20, 2009 (re-elected 2004).

standing.basis: Gallup: Bush averaged 62.1% job approval over his first term (yearly averages 67.1%, 71.4%, 59.6% and 50.1%), within the 50-65% band.

education.basis: Yale University BA in history (1968) and Harvard Business School MBA (1975), so a professional/master's degree was held throughout.

phases.label: President, second term
phases.summary: Bush served a second presidential term from January 20, 2005, to January 20, 2009, covering the Iraq troop surge, implementation of Medicare Part D, and the 2008 financial crisis response including TARP.

health.basis: 2007 physical: 'healthy overall', fitness 'superior' for age, each examiner found him fit for duty. Early localized Lyme disease (rash) was treated in Aug 2006 with no recurrence; July 2007 colonoscopy removed five small polyps (all under 1 cm), benign on pathology. Minor, treated findings.

social.basis: Evidence is divided. Dee and Jacob (NBER 15531) found NCLB gains in 4th and 8th grade math, none in reading, measured to 2007. PEPFAR was associated with lower adult mortality (OR 0.84; Hein et al. 2020 replication, disputed by an earlier study). Iraq Family Health Survey (WHO/NEJM 2008): 151,000 violent deaths Mar 2003-Jun 2006, overlapping Jan 2005-Jun 2006; later years not covered by that survey.

wealth.basis: Adjusted gross income was $765,801 (2006) and $923,807 (2007) per NBC's report of the White House return releases. IRS SOI Bulletin Winter 2010 Table 5 AGI floors: top 1% $388,806 (2006) and $410,096 (2007); top 0.1% $2,044,689 and $2,155,365. Income was above the top-1% floor and below the top-0.1% floor.

economic.basis: Mixed. CBO (2014) found Part D spending in 2013 about half its 2003 projection, from slower drug-spending growth and lower enrollment, with lower costs where more sponsors competed. CBO estimated the TARP net cost at $34B (Dec 2011) against $700B authorized. Deficit was $458B in FY2008 after a $128B surplus in FY2001 (CRS/AP). Evidence divided.

position.basis: Head of state and government as President of the United States, second term January 20, 2005 to January 20, 2009.

standing.basis: Gallup: Bush averaged 36.5% job approval over the second term to January 2009 (a 25% low in late 2008; 34% final reading in Jan 2009), within the 35-50% band.

education.basis: Yale University BA in history (1968) and Harvard Business School MBA (1975), so a professional/master's degree was held throughout.

misconduct.basis: 1 documented matter(s) in the reviewed legal record, counted as the misconduct meter counts them.

phases.label: President, 1789-1797
phases.summary: Led the new federal government through two unanimous elections, the creation of the Treasury, bank, mint and federal courts, and the suppression of the Whiskey Rebellion. Held enslaved people throughout and freed those he owned only by will.

social.basis: Judiciary Act of 1789 and the Bill of Rights period created courts and rights protections, but he directed the Northwest Indian War expanding control over tribal lands and held more than 100 enslaved people at Mount Vernon (freed 123-124 only by will after his death). Mixed to negative on rights.

economic.basis: Funding Act of 1790 assumed state debts (about $79 million combined debt), the First Bank of the United States (1791), the Coinage Act of 1792 and customs service established a functioning fiscal base; import duties supplied over 87% of revenue 1789-1800. The excise tax triggered the Whiskey Rebellion and protective manufacturing proposals largely failed.

position.basis: First president of the United States, elected unanimously by the electoral college in 1789 and 1792 (69 and 132 electoral votes).

education.basis: Did not receive the formal schooling of his half-brothers; attended a local church school and taught himself mathematics and surveying.

misconduct.basis: No official finding, court ruling or ethics action against him appears in the presidency article; the House's demand for Jay Treaty papers was refused on executive-privilege grounds, not adjudicated as misconduct.

phases.label: President, 1974-1977
phases.summary: Succeeded after Nixon's resignation, pardoned Nixon, governed through the worst recession since the Depression, signed the Helsinki Accords and special-education law, and narrowly lost in 1976.

social.basis: Education for All Handicapped Children Act (1975) established special education nationwide; about 130,000 Vietnamese refugees admitted in 1975 with $455 million resettlement funding; Helsinki Accords. The 1976 swine-flu programme vaccinated about 25% of the population and was alleged linked to 25 deaths before cancellation.

economic.basis: Inherited stagflation: inflation over 12% in 1974 and unemployment 9% in May 1975, worst recession since the Depression; WIN campaign was ineffective, the Tax Reduction Act of 1975 cut taxes and inflation/unemployment declined in 1976, but deficits were $53.2 billion (FY1975) and $73.7 billion (FY1976).

position.basis: 38th president, serving August 1974 to January 1977; lost the 1976 election 48.0% to 50.1%.

standing.basis: Gallup average job approval of 47% (range 37-71%); fell 21 points after the Nixon pardon on September 8, 1974.

education.basis: University of Michigan B.A. in economics (1935) and Yale Law School LL.B. (1941).

misconduct.basis: The pardon was widely criticised but no court, congressional ethics finding or regulator action against him is recorded in the sources opened (he testified voluntarily to the House on October 17, 1974).

phases.label: Sheriff of Erie County, Mayor of Buffalo, Governor of New York
phases.summary: Rapid rise through Buffalo and state politics on a reform reputation.

position.basis: Governor of New York 1 January 1883 - 6 January 1885, after Mayor of Buffalo (1882) and Erie County sheriff (1871-73).

education.basis: Left school after his father's death in 1853; read law and was admitted to the New York bar in 1859 (no college).

phases.label: President, first term
phases.summary: Record veto use, the Interstate Commerce Act, the Dawes Act and a tariff-reduction message that cost him re-election.

social.basis: Mixed: Interstate Commerce Act 1887 created the first independent federal regulatory agency, but he signed the Dawes Act (Native landholdings fell from 155 million acres in 1881 to 77 million in 1900) and vetoed the Texas Seed Bill and hundreds of veterans' pension bills.

position.basis: Head of state and government March 1885 - March 1889.

phases.label: President, second term
phases.summary: Panic of 1893 and depression, repeal of the Sherman Silver Purchase Act, gold-reserve crisis, the Pullman Strike injunction and a secret cancer operation.

health.basis: Secret operation on 1 July 1893 aboard the yacht Oneida to remove an oral tumour, disfiguring the mouth and needing a rubber prosthesis; hidden from the public until 1917.

social.basis: Federal injunction and troops in Chicago and 20 other rail centres against the 125,000-worker Pullman Strike in 1894; unemployment above 20% in much of the country during the depression.

economic.basis: Panic of 1893: hundreds of banks failed and 25% of railroads were in receivership by 1895; Sherman Silver Purchase Act repealed (House 239-108) and a $60M J.P. Morgan bond sale shored up gold; Wilson-Gorman Tariff cut average rates from 49% to 42% while its income tax was struck down in 1895.

position.basis: Head of state and government March 1893 - March 1897.

phases.label: President, 1945-1953
phases.summary: Ended World War II, launched the Marshall Plan and NATO, desegregated the armed forces, and left office unpopular after the Korean War, the steel seizure and corruption scandals.

social.basis: Executive Order 9981 (1948) required equal opportunity in the armed forces and EO 9980 barred discrimination in federal hiring; the Displaced Persons Act of 1948 admitted over 400,000 refugees; Housing Act of 1949. Offset by the atomic bombings (about 135,000 killed immediately) and the Korean War (over 30,000 Americans killed).

economic.basis: Demobilization cut military spending from 39% of GNP (1945) to 5% (1948); Marshall Plan allocated $12.4 billion and European industrial productivity was 35% above 1938 by 1952; Fair Deal economic proposals were largely blocked and Taft-Hartley passed over his veto. No unemployment or inflation figures in the sources opened.

position.basis: 33rd president; elected in his own right in 1948 and head of state through the end of the war and the Korean War.

standing.basis: Gallup average job approval of 45% (high 87%, low 22% in February 1952, the lowest Gallup mark for a sitting president until Nixon matched it).

education.basis: Graduated Independence High School (1901), attended a commercial college for about a year and night law classes at Kansas City Law School 1923-1925 without a degree; the only president since McKinley without a college degree.

misconduct.basis: In Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952) the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that his April 1952 seizure of steel mills lacked statutory or constitutional basis. A 1950 Senate (Kefauver) investigation and internal revenue resignations touched subordinates rather than Truman personally.

phases.label: Mining engineer, relief administrator and Secretary of Commerce
phases.summary: Global mining career, Commission for Relief in Belgium, US Food Administration, American Relief Administration and eight years at Commerce.

social.basis: The Commission for Relief in Belgium distributed over two million tons of food to nine million war victims; the European Children's Fund aided about fifteen million children in fourteen countries; ARA Russian famine relief is said to have saved millions.

wealth.basis: Estimated personal fortune of $4 million by 1914, compared with a first salary of $5,000 a year as a mine scout in the 1890s. No period distribution threshold was opened, so placement near the top 0.1% is a judgement.

position.basis: Secretary of Commerce 1921-1928 and chairman of the Commission for Relief in Belgium and director of the Food and American Relief Administrations.

education.basis: BS in geology from Stanford 1895, one of its first graduates.

phases.label: President of the United States
phases.summary: The stock market crash and Great Depression, Smoot-Hawley Tariff, the RFC and the Bonus Army, ending in a 1932 landslide defeat.

social.basis: Unemployment reached 11.9% by end-1930 and nearly 23% in early 1932; two Bonus Army protesters were killed and he endorsed clearing the camp; the Emergency Relief and Construction Act ($2B public works) and RFC were modest counter-measures.

economic.basis: GNP fell about 30% between 1928 and 1932; Smoot-Hawley raised average industrial duties from 31% to 34% and drew retaliation; money supply contracted; national debt rose from about 20% to 40% of GNP; the Revenue Act of 1932 raised the top rate from 25% to 63%.

position.basis: Head of state and government 4 March 1929 - 4 March 1933.

phases.label: Former President and Hoover Commission chair
phases.summary: Critic of the New Deal, then Truman's Commission on Organization of the Executive Branch and postwar food relief for Germany.

health.basis: Three major illnesses in his last two years, including August 1962 intestinal surgery; died 20 October 1964 aged 90 from internal bleeding.

social.basis: 1946-47 postwar food missions and a school meals programme in the US and British zones of Germany serving 3.5 million children; Hoover Commission recommendations partly adopted by Truman.

phases.label: Ohio senator, Union general, nine-term US Representative
phases.summary: Ohio State Senate, Union Army major general, then the US House from 1863 until his election as president.

position.basis: Nine terms in the US House (March 1863 - November 1880) and elected to the US Senate before taking the presidency.

education.basis: Graduated Williams College August 1856 (Phi Beta Kappa, salutatorian).

misconduct.basis: Named in the Crédit Mobilier inquiry (1873): the House censured Oakes Ames and James Brooks but took no action against Garfield and no charges were filed; biographers say he was not fully candid about a $329 dividend.

phases.label: President of the United States
phases.summary: About four months in office, dominated by the fight with Roscoe Conkling over patronage, until he was shot on 2 July 1881.

health.basis: Shot by Charles Guiteau on 2 July 1881 and died 79 days later on 19 September 1881 of a massive infection including sepsis and pneumonia.

position.basis: Head of state and government 4 March - 19 September 1881.

misconduct.basis: 1 documented matter(s) in the reviewed legal record, counted as the misconduct meter counts them.

phases.label: President, one term
phases.summary: Faced the Panic of 1857, the Lecompton crisis and the secession of seven states before leaving office; a House committee investigated his administration.

health.basis: Contracted severe dysentery in January 1857 at the National Hotel and did not fully recover for several months.

social.basis: Vetoed the Homestead Act and the Morrill land-grant college act in 1859-60; supported the Lecompton pro-slavery constitution; sent the army into Utah on uncorroborated reports; seven states seceded before he left. Judgement-heavy.

economic.basis: Panic of 1857: about 1,400 state banks and 5,000 businesses failed; his policy was 'reform not relief'; the deficit was $17M when he left office; the economy recovered by 1859.

position.basis: President of the United States, 1857-1861.
