education.basis: Graduated with honors from Dickinson College in 1809, read law in Lancaster and passed the bar in 1812.

misconduct.basis: 1 documented matter(s) in the reviewed legal record, counted as the misconduct meter counts them.

phases.label: President, one term
phases.summary: Added Texas, Oregon and the Mexican Cession through annexation, treaty and war, and cut tariffs; the House voted that the war had been begun unconstitutionally.

social.basis: Mexican-American War killed nearly 14,000 Americans and 25,000 Mexicans; the Mexican Cession (600,000 sq mi) reopened the fight over slavery's extension (Wilmot Proviso); the Oregon dispute was settled by treaty without war. Judgement-heavy.

economic.basis: Walker Tariff of 1846 substantially reduced rates and lasted until 1857; Independent Treasury Act (Aug 6, 1846) lasted until 1913; the war cost roughly $100M. The source gives no revenue or growth figures.

position.basis: President of the United States, 1845-1849.

education.basis: Graduated from the University of North Carolina (AB, with honors, 1818), then studied law under Felix Grundy and was admitted to the Tennessee bar in June 1820.

phases.label: President, two terms
phases.summary: Led the country through the War of 1812, chartered the Second Bank of the United States and vetoed the Bonus Bill.

health.basis: Had episodes of mental exhaustion and sudden attacks 'consistent with today's understanding of epilepsy', but enjoyed good physical health until his final years.

social.basis: War of 1812 followed a failed embargo; the U.S. acquired 26,000,000 acres from Native American tribes by treaty or war during his presidency; Washington was burned in August 1814. Judgement-heavy.

economic.basis: Chartered the Second Bank of the United States for 25 years (government held one-fifth of the capital), signed the protective Tariff of 1816, vetoed the Bonus Bill for internal improvements in 1817. No debt or growth figures in the source.

position.basis: President of the United States, 1809-1817.

education.basis: Enrolled at the College of New Jersey (Princeton) in 1769 and completed its three-year BA in two years, graduating in 1771.

phases.label: President, two terms
phases.summary: Era of Good Feelings: Missouri Compromise, acquisition of Florida and the Monroe Doctrine, with the Panic of 1819.

social.basis: Signed the Missouri Compromise (Missouri a slave state, slavery barred north of 36 30'); acquired Florida under the Adams-Onis Treaty (1819); Panic of 1819 brought unemployment, bankruptcies and foreclosures. Judgement-heavy.

economic.basis: The Panic of 1819 is called the first major depression in U.S. history; he signed the General Survey Act (1824) and Tariff of 1824 but vetoed a bill for National Road tolls in 1822. No debt or growth figures in the source.

position.basis: President of the United States, 1817-1825.

education.basis: Enrolled at the College of William & Mary in June 1774 (the source states no degree), then studied law under Thomas Jefferson 1780-1783.

misconduct.basis: 1 documented matter(s) in the reviewed legal record, counted as the misconduct meter counts them.

phases.label: Georgia state senator and Governor of Georgia
phases.summary: State senate 1963-1967, then governor of Georgia from January 1971 to January 1975.

position.basis: 76th Governor of Georgia, 12 January 1971 - 14 January 1975.

education.basis: BS, US Naval Academy 1946, plus a six-month nuclear power plant operation course at Union College in 1953; no graduate degree documented in the page.

phases.label: President of the United States
phases.summary: Camp David Accords and Panama Canal treaties, deregulation and energy policy, undercut by stagflation and the Iran hostage crisis.

social.basis: Alaska lands legislation doubled park and refuge acreage, Superfund created in 1980, National Energy Act 1978; per-capita energy use fell 10% 1979-83 and oil imports halved. Historians rank the presidency below average overall (26th in 2017 C-SPAN).

economic.basis: Mixed: unemployment fell from 7.5% (Jan 1977) to 5.6% (May 1979) with over 9 million net new jobs, then 7.8% in 1980; inflation rose from 5.8% (1976) to 13.5% (1980); airline, trucking, rail and banking deregulation passed; deficits near $70B a year.

position.basis: Head of state and government 20 January 1977 - 20 January 1981.

standing.basis: Gallup job approval averaged 45.5% over the term; peak 75% (March 1977), low 28% (June 1979).

misconduct.basis: Special counsel Paul Curran reported in October 1979 no evidence peanut-business loans were diverted to Carter's 1976 campaign; the Senate investigated Billy Carter's Libya payments with the president having no personal involvement; OMB director Lance resigned in 1977. No finding against Carter.

phases.label: Former President and Carter Center founder
phases.summary: Carter Center work on disease eradication and election monitoring, Nobel Peace Prize 2002, and a record-length life ending at 100.

health.basis: Melanoma found in liver and brain in August 2015, no cancer on scans by December 2015; hip fracture and several falls in 2019, brain-pressure procedure November 2019; hospice care from February 2023; died 29 December 2024 aged 100, the longest-lived US president.

social.basis: Carter Center has worked on Guinea worm eradication since 1986, when WHO estimated 3.5 million cases a year in 20 countries; human cases fell to 13-15 a year in 2022-2024. Attribution shared with WHO and many partners.

standing.basis: Gallup: Carter averaged 45.5% job approval across his presidency (35-50% band); essentially tied with Truman as second lowest among post-WWII presidents. Gallup, published Dec 2024.

misconduct.basis: 2 documented matter(s) in the reviewed legal record, counted as the misconduct meter counts them.

phases.label: Senate years
phases.summary: Biden served as U.S. Senator from Delaware from January 1973 to January 2009, chairing the Judiciary Committee (1987-1995) and, in 2001-2003 and 2007-2009, the Foreign Relations Committee.

health.basis: Surgery in February 1988 for a leaking intracranial aneurysm and a second repair in May 1988. Records released in October 2008 described the two aneurysm treatments and otherwise mostly minor problems (back pain, chronic sinusitis, seasonal allergies); no recurrence is described. Serious treated condition (2) with no ongoing impairment documented, so scored 2.5.

social.basis: Biden was lead sponsor of S.11 (VAWA, 103rd Congress) and chaired Judiciary during the 1994 crime law. BJS: intimate-partner violence fell 64% 1994-2010, with no attribution to any law. Brennan Center (2016): the law's police funding likely helped, its prison provisions had limited effect on crime; evidence is divided.

wealth.basis: Joint adjusted gross income was $269,256 in 2008 (White House release) and $319,853 in 2007 (Tax Notes table). IRS SOI floors: 2008 top 5% $163,512, top 1% $392,513; 2007 top 5% $164,883, top 1% $426,439. Income sat between the top-5% and top-1% floors. Only 2007-08 returns are documented for this 36-year phase.

position.basis: U.S. senator from Delaware for six terms: a statewide elected national legislative office, with chairmanships of the Judiciary (1987-95) and Foreign Relations (2001-03, 2007-09) committees; scored 4 under 'statewide or national-level office'.

education.basis: Holds a B.A. from the University of Delaware (1965) and a J.D. from Syracuse University College of Law (1968), both obtained before he took office; a professional law degree scores 4.

phases.label: Vice president
phases.summary: Biden served as Vice President under Barack Obama from 20 January 2009 to 20 January 2017, including oversight of Recovery Act implementation.

health.basis: A December 2019 physician report (Dr. Kevin O'Connor, his primary physician since 2009) records atrial fibrillation episodes since 2003 treated with a blood thinner, cholesterol controlled with a statin, no aneurysm recurrence on a 2014 arterial test, and small skin cancers removed. No vice-presidential annual summary was located, so this is retrospective.

wealth.basis: Joint AGI was $379,178 in 2010 and $392,233 in 2015 (White House releases), $407,009 in 2013 and $396,456 in 2016 (Tax Notes). IRS SOI 2010 floors: top 5% $161,579, top 1% $369,691. Census H-1 top-5% household limit: $191,200 (2012), $225,300 (2016). Income was in the top 5%, near the top-1% floor in 2010.

economic.basis: Biden was assigned to oversee Recovery Act implementation (Feb 2009). CBO estimated the Act raised 2010 real GDP by 0.7 to 4.1% and lowered the unemployment rate by 0.4 to 1.8 points, at a cost of about $836 billion. The IGM panel mostly agreed it lowered unemployment but was divided on whether benefits exceeded costs. Scored leaning beneficial; he did not author the Act.

position.basis: Vice President of the United States and presiding officer of the Senate: the second-highest national office, below head of state or government.

standing.basis: Gallup favorability readings were 42% (Oct 2009), 44% (Sep 2012) and 49% (2015), with Americans 'about evenly divided' from late 2009 to early 2015 and a 61% peak in his final days in office. No full-term average is published; readings sit in the 35-50% band.

education.basis: Holds a B.A. from the University of Delaware (1965) and a J.D. from Syracuse University College of Law (1968), both obtained before he took office; a professional law degree scores 4.

phases.label: President
phases.summary: Biden served as the 46th President of the United States from 20 January 2021 to 20 January 2025.

health.basis: Annual White House physician reports (Dr. Kevin O'Connor) list atrial fibrillation (asymptomatic on medication), cholesterol managed with medication, reflux, spinal arthritis with a stiff gait, and from 2023 sleep apnea treated with CPAP; each report found him fit for duty. Managed chronic conditions score 3.

social.basis: Census: the SPM child poverty rate was a record-low 5.2% in 2021 and rose to 12.4% in 2022; refundable tax credits lifted 9.6 million people out of poverty in 2021 and 6.4 million in 2022. CDC: the uninsured rate was 7.6% in 2023, down from 8.4% in 2022. Beneficial effects were partly temporary; no outcome evaluation of other domains was reviewed. Coverage limited to poverty and insurance.

wealth.basis: Joint 2021 AGI was $610,702 (White House release; salary $378,333 for the part-year). Tax Foundation's IRS-based 2021 floors: top 5% $252,840, top 1% $682,577. Census H-1 top-5% household limit for 2021 was $286,300. Income was above the top-5% floor and below the top-1% floor; net worth was not used.

economic.basis: CBO scores of the signature laws: American Rescue Plan about +$1.8 trillion deficit (2021-31), Inflation Reduction Act -$238 billion, CHIPS and Science Act +$79 billion, and infrastructure law growth effects of under 0.1% of GDP in CBO's generic analysis. Fiscal and growth effects point in different directions and are contested, so the net is scored as mixed.

position.basis: President of the United States: head of state and head of government.

standing.basis: Gallup's average job approval for his term was 42.2%, the second lowest in its records; his last reading was 40%. That falls in the 35-50% band.

education.basis: Holds a B.A. from the University of Delaware (1965) and a J.D. from Syracuse University College of Law (1968), both obtained before he took office; a professional law degree scores 4.

misconduct.basis: A Special Counsel investigation of retained classified documents opened on 12 January 2023 and ended with the 5 February 2024 report concluding that no criminal charges are warranted and the evidence does not establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. One matter, resolved in his favour.

phases.label: President, 1797-1801
phases.summary: Kept the United States out of declared war with France during the Quasi-War and built the navy, but signed the Alien and Sedition Acts and lost the 1800 election.

social.basis: Naturalization Act raised residency for citizenship from 5 to 14 years, the Sedition Act criminalized criticism of the government (about 10 convictions, newspapers sued), though he signed the Slave Trade Act of 1800 and pardoned Fries. Net negative on rights.

economic.basis: Built a navy (from one revenue boat) and the Direct Tax of 1798 funded defence but provoked Fries's Rebellion; no debt or growth figures were available, so judged mixed.

position.basis: Second president of the United States, 1797-1801; lost the 1800 election after the House decided it on the 36th ballot.

education.basis: Harvard A.B. 1755 and A.M. 1758, read law and admitted to the bar in 1759.

phases.label: President, 1961-1963
phases.summary: Presided over strong growth, the Cuban Missile Crisis, the Peace Corps and a late push for civil rights legislation before his assassination.

health.basis: Addison's disease diagnosed in September 1947 and treated with corticosteroids, chronic severe back pain with surgery, and treatment with amphetamines and steroids judged medically inappropriate by physician George Burkley; much was concealed at the time.

social.basis: EO 10925 required affirmative action by contractors, EO 11063 barred housing discrimination, he sent marshals and troops to Freedom Riders and Ole Miss and proposed the civil rights bill in June 1963; early reluctance, FBI wiretaps on King, and an 18-fold increase in Vietnam advisers temper the score. Peace Corps sent 100,000 Americans abroad over 25 years.

economic.basis: GDP grew an average 5.5% a year from early 1961 to late 1963 versus 2.2% under Eisenhower, inflation stayed near 1% and industrial production rose 15%; his tax-cut proposal passed in 1964 after his death. The 1961 budget produced the first non-war non-recession deficit.

position.basis: 35th president of the United States, 1961 to November 22, 1963.

standing.basis: Gallup average job approval of 70% (range 56-82%); approval rose from 66% to 77% after the Cuban Missile Crisis.

education.basis: Harvard B.A. in government, cum laude, 1940; audited one semester at Stanford business school.

misconduct.basis: The sources opened report no official findings of misconduct against him; the Profiles in Courage authorship question is not an official action.

phases.label: President, one term
phases.summary: Pursued roads, canals and science institutions against a hostile Congress and lost to Jackson in 1828.

social.basis: Suspended the 1825 Treaty of Indian Springs after Georgia forced it on the Muscogee; proposals for a national university, observatory and naval academy were defeated 86-78 or never voted on. Judgement-heavy.

economic.basis: National Road reached Zanesville, the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal was begun and the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad built during his term; he signed the 'Tariff of Abominations' (House 105-94). The source gives no dollar figures.

position.basis: President of the United States, 1825-1829.

education.basis: Graduated from Harvard College in 1787, second in his class, and studied law under Theophilus Parsons 1787-1789.

misconduct.basis: The 'corrupt bargain' charge over Henry Clay's appointment was a political accusation; the presidency article reports no official investigation.

phases.label: President, 1841-1845
phases.summary: First vice president to succeed on a president's death; vetoed Whig national bank bills, was expelled from his party, and signed the annexation of Texas on his last full days in office.

social.basis: Texas annexation (approved 27-25 in the Senate, signed March 1, 1845) extended slave territory; Webster-Ashburton Treaty pledged stronger action against the slave trade and the Second Seminole War ended in 1842. He held enslaved people throughout and later served the Confederacy.

economic.basis: Vetoed two national-bank bills and repealed the Independent Treasury, signed the Bankruptcy Act of 1841 and the Tariff of 1842 (restoring 1832 rates); his Exchequer Plan was not adopted. The economy was still recovering from the Panic of 1837; no growth figures available.

position.basis: Tenth president of the United States, serving 1841-1845 after William Henry Harrison's death.

education.basis: Graduated from the collegiate branch of the College of William and Mary in 1807 and read law with his father and Edmund Randolph; no postgraduate degree.

misconduct.basis: 1 documented matter(s) in the reviewed legal record, counted as the misconduct meter counts them.

phases.label: President, 1963-1969
phases.summary: Signed the Civil Rights Act, Voting Rights Act, Medicare and Medicaid and the Great Society programmes while escalating the Vietnam War from about 16,000 to over 500,000 troops.

health.basis: Near-fatal heart attack in July 1955 (smoked about 60 cigarettes a day) and gallbladder and kidney-stone surgery at Bethesda in November 1965; no incapacity documented in the term.

social.basis: Civil Rights Act 1964, Voting Rights Act 1965 (Mississippi Black registration 6.7% to 59.8% 1964-67), Medicare enrolled about 19 million in 1966, ESEA, Head Start, and the poverty rate fell from about 20% (1964) to 12% (1974). Vietnam casualties and urban unrest excluded from this domestic assessment.

economic.basis: GDP rose from about $661.7 billion (1964) to $980.3 billion (1969), the Revenue Act of 1964 cut the top rate from 91% to 70% and debt fell from 38.8% to 28.4% of GDP; inflation rose with Vietnam and domestic spending and the FY1968 deficit was $25.2 billion.

position.basis: 36th president, succeeded on November 22, 1963 and elected in 1964.

standing.basis: Gallup average job approval of 55% (range 35-79%); fell below 50% through 1966-67 and bottomed at 35%.

education.basis: B.S. in history from Southwest Texas State Teachers College, 1930, with a high school teaching certificate.

phases.label: President, one term
phases.summary: Presided over the Panic of 1837 and its depression, created the Independent Treasury and oversaw the 1838 removal of the Cherokee.

social.basis: Ordered the 1838 removal of Cherokee under the 1835 Treaty of New Echota ('some 20,000 people' relocated); the Second Seminole War cost over 1,400 American servicemen; he issued a ten-hour-day order for federal workers in 1840. Judgement-heavy.

economic.basis: Panic of 1837 began May 10, 1837 and was followed by a five-year depression with numerous bank failures and record unemployment; he won the Independent Treasury in June 1840 and kept the budget balanced.

position.basis: President of the United States, 1837-1841.

education.basis: Village schoolhouse, then briefly Latin at Kinderhook Academy and Washington Seminary; formal education ended in 1796 when he began reading law; no college. Admitted to the New York bar by 1803.

misconduct.basis: The presidency article describes no formal investigation or official finding; historian Laurence Hauptman's claim that the 1838 Treaty of Buffalo Creek was fraudulently imposed is an allegation, not an official finding.

phases.label: President, from Taylor's death
phases.summary: Signed the Compromise of 1850 including the Fugitive Slave Act and backed the Perry expedition to Japan.

social.basis: Signed and enforced the Fugitive Slave Act (federal commissioners, no jury trial, defendants could not testify, penalties for aiding fugitives); the Compromise also banned the slave trade in Washington, D.C. and admitted California as a free state. Judgement-heavy.

position.basis: President of the United States, July 1850 to March 1853.

education.basis: Biographer Tyler Anbinder describes 'virtually no formal schooling'; he read law under Judge Walter Wood and was admitted to the bar in 1823. No college degree.

misconduct.basis: The presidency article mentions no investigation or official finding against Fillmore.

phases.label: President, first term 1969-1973
phases.summary: Created the EPA and OSHA, signed the Clean Air Act and Endangered Species Act, ended the draft and Bretton Woods convertibility, and won re-election with 61% of the vote.

social.basis: Created the EPA, signed the Clean Air Act, Endangered Species Act and OSHA; fewer than 10% of Black children attended segregated schools by September 1970; poverty fell from 12.8% (1968) to 11.1% (1973); Family Assistance Plan failed. Vietnam combat ended in 1973.

economic.basis: Imposed wage and price controls (August 1971), ended dollar-gold convertibility, and the first negative trade balance of the century occurred in 1971; unemployment rose from 3.5% to 5.6% and inflation from 4.7% to 8.7% by 1974, producing stagflation.

position.basis: 37th president; won 520 electoral votes and 60.7% of the popular vote in 1972.

education.basis: Whittier College B.A. (1934) and Duke University LL.B. (1937), third in his class.

phases.label: Watergate and resignation, 1973-1974
phases.summary: The Watergate cover-up unravelled through court rulings, congressional hearings and the House Judiciary Committee's impeachment articles, ending in his resignation on August 9, 1974.

economic.basis: Wage-price controls were reimposed in June 1973 and lapsed April 1974; the 1973 OPEC embargo caused shortages and rationing; inflation reached 8.7% and unemployment 5.6% by 1974.

position.basis: Held the presidency until his resignation on August 9, 1974, the only president to resign.

standing.basis: Final Gallup reading 24% in August 1974, within 2 points of Truman's 22% record low; Gallup average across the whole presidency 49% (range 24-67%).

education.basis: Whittier College B.A. (1934) and Duke University LL.B. (1937).

misconduct.basis: House Judiciary Committee recommended impeachment on obstruction of justice, abuse of power and contempt of Congress; Supreme Court unanimously ordered the tapes released on July 24, 1974; 69 people charged and 48 officials convicted in the scandal; paid $465,000 in back taxes in 1974. Disbarment came in 1976, after the phase.

phases.label: President, 1981-1989
phases.summary: Cut taxes and curbed inflation after the 1981-82 recession, tripled the national debt, expanded defence spending, and weathered the Iran-Contra affair; left office with 63-68% approval.

health.basis: Shot by John Hinckley on March 30, 1981 (broken rib, punctured lung, internal bleeding, surgery); colon cancer surgery removing two feet of upper colon on July 13, 1985.

social.basis: Did not publicly mention AIDS for months in 1985-86, by 1989 about 60,000 Americans had died, and Congress funded $5.6 billion versus the $2.8 billion proposed; Anti-Drug Abuse Act mandatory minimums with racial disparities; vetoed the Civil Rights Restoration Act (overridden); IRCA gave amnesty to about 3 million.

economic.basis: Unemployment peaked at 10.8% (December 1982) and fell to 5.3% by 1989; inflation fell from about 12% to under 5%; longest peacetime expansion to that date; but the national debt tripled from $914 billion to $2.7 trillion and deficits peaked at $221.2 billion in FY1986.

position.basis: 40th president; re-elected in a landslide over Mondale in 1984.

standing.basis: Gallup average job approval of 53% (range 35-68%); low in the mid-30s in 1982-83, final reading 63% (Wikipedia presidency article gives 68% for another poll).

education.basis: Eureka College B.A. in economics and sociology, 1932.

misconduct.basis: 1 documented matter(s) in the reviewed legal record, counted as the misconduct meter counts them.

phases.label: Union general, US Representative and Governor of Ohio
phases.summary: Five-times-wounded Civil War officer, one House term, then governor of Ohio 1868-72 and 1876-77.

health.basis: Wounded five times in the Civil War, the worst at South Mountain in 1862 (left arm bone fractured); a doctor suspected tuberculosis in 1847.

position.basis: Governor of Ohio 1868-1872 and again January 1876 - March 1877.

education.basis: Kenyon College 1842 (valedictorian) and LLB, Harvard Law School, admitted to the Ohio bar in 1845.

phases.label: President of the United States
phases.summary: Disputed 1876 election, withdrawal of federal troops ending Reconstruction, the 1877 railroad strike, specie resumption in 1879 and modest civil service reform.

social.basis: Withdrew federal troops from South Carolina (10 April 1877) and Louisiana (29 April 1877), ending Reconstruction; used troops in the Great Railroad Strike; vetoed the 1879 Fifteen Passenger Bill; modest civil service reform preceded the Pendleton Act.

economic.basis: Specie payments resumed on 1 January 1879 with only $130,000 of $346M in greenbacks redeemed; vetoed the inflationary Bland-Allison Act (override); the article describes prosperity for the rest of his term.

position.basis: Head of state and government 4 March 1877 - 4 March 1881.

misconduct.basis: The Electoral Commission awarded him all 20 disputed votes (8-7); a House attempt at impeachment failed when Republicans denied a quorum; the Star Route postal probe found no connection to Hayes. No finding against him.

phases.label: Reformer: Assemblyman, Civil Service Commissioner, Police Commissioner, Governor
phases.summary: From the New York Assembly through the Civil Service Commission, NYC police commissionership and the New York governorship.

position.basis: Governor of New York January 1899 - December 1900, after serving as Assistant Secretary of the Navy and NYC Police Commissioner.

education.basis: AB Harvard 1880 (magna cum laude, Phi Beta Kappa); attended Columbia Law School but left in 1881 without a degree.

phases.label: President of the United States
phases.summary: Square Deal: trust-busting, food and drug regulation, large-scale conservation, the Panama Canal and a Nobel Peace Prize.

social.basis: Pure Food and Drug Act and Meat Inspection Act (1906); about 230 million acres brought under federal protection, 150 national forests, five national parks and 18 national monuments; 1902 coal strike commission cut the miners' day to nine hours; offset by the Brownsville mass discharge of Black soldiers.

economic.basis: Northern Securities (1904) and Standard Oil suit; Hepburn Act (Senate 71-3) extended ICC rate powers; the Panic of 1907 was the worst crisis since 1893 and needed a private J.P. Morgan rescue, leading to the Aldrich-Vreeland Act and later the Federal Reserve.

position.basis: Head of state and government 14 September 1901 - 4 March 1909.

phases.label: Former President: Bull Moose campaign and River of Doubt
phases.summary: 1912 third-party run (shot in Milwaukee) and the 1913-14 Amazon expedition that damaged his health.

health.basis: Shot in the chest in Milwaukee on 14 October 1912 and carried the bullet for life; nearly died of a tropical disease on the Amazon expedition; died 6 January 1919 aged 60.

misconduct.basis: 1 documented matter(s) in the reviewed legal record, counted as the misconduct meter counts them.

phases.label: President, two terms
phases.summary: Cut the national debt and doubled the country's area with the Louisiana Purchase, but the 1807 Embargo Act damaged trade.

social.basis: Called for and saw enacted the ban on the international slave trade (effective January 1808; the legal trade had averaged about 14,000 a year, with about 1,000 a year smuggled afterwards); Louisiana Purchase of 827,987 sq mi; but the Embargo Act hurt coastal communities and slavery expanded west. Judgement-heavy.

economic.basis: National debt lowered from $83M to $57M and internal taxes repealed (over 90% of revenue from import duties); Louisiana Purchase cost $15M financed by borrowing; Embargo Act made imports and exports 'fall immensely' and Joseph Ellis calls it 'an unadulterated calamity'.

position.basis: President of the United States, head of state and government, 1801-1809.

education.basis: Entered the College of William & Mary in 1761 and concluded formal studies in April 1762; no degree is mentioned. He then read law under George Wythe.

misconduct.basis: The presidency article records no impeachment or formal investigation of Jefferson himself; his Burr-trial subpoena was met by releasing some documents under executive privilege. Impeachments in the period (Pickering, Chase) targeted judges.

phases.label: Commanding General of the US Army
phases.summary: General-in-chief of the Union armies from March 1864 and Commanding General until he became president.

position.basis: Commanding General of the US Army 9 March 1864 - 4 March 1869 (top uniformed role).

education.basis: Graduated West Point 30 June 1843, ranked 21st of 39 (an academy course, no bachelor's degree conferred).

phases.label: President of the United States
phases.summary: Reconstruction enforcement against the Klan, the Fifteenth Amendment, the creation of the Justice Department, the Panic of 1873 and a series of administration scandals.

social.basis: Fifteenth Amendment ratified February 1870; roughly 1,000 Klan indictments and over 550 convictions; Department of Justice created; Civil Rights Act of 1875 largely unenforced and struck down in 1883; Indian wars fell from 101 (1869) to 15 (1875) but Marias Massacre killed 173 Piegan.

economic.basis: Panic of 1873 began a depression of about five years with unemployment reaching 14% and wages down 25% for three years; Resumption Act of 1875 (effective 1 January 1879) and debt paydown were the administration's main fiscal moves.

position.basis: Head of state and government 4 March 1869 - 4 March 1877.

phases.label: Private citizen, Grant & Ward and the Memoirs
phases.summary: World tour, business failure in 1884 and the race to finish his memoirs while dying of throat cancer.

health.basis: Dying of throat cancer in 1885 while writing his memoirs; died 23 July 1885 aged 63 at Grant Cottage, Moreau, New York.

phases.label: President, died in office
phases.summary: Created the federal budget system, cut taxes and held the Washington Naval Conference; scandals broke around his administration and he died in August 1923.

health.basis: Aware of a heart condition by 1919; never fully recovered from influenza in January 1923; doctors found heart trouble and pneumonia on July 29, 1923 and he died of an apparent heart attack on August 2, 1923, aged 57.

social.basis: Signed the Sheppard-Towner Maternity Act (almost 3,000 child and health centers), commuted Eugene Debs's sentence and publicly deplored the steel industry's 12-hour day; against that, he signed the 1921 Emergency Quota Act and the Dyer anti-lynching bill died in the Senate in November 1922. Judgement-heavy.

economic.basis: Budget and Accounting Act (June 1921) created the Bureau of the Budget; spending fell $1.5B (25%) in the first budget director's first year and another 25% the next; Revenue Act of 1921 cut the top rate from 73% to 58%; unemployment was about 11% in 1922.

position.basis: President of the United States, March 1921 to August 1923.

education.basis: Enrolled at Ohio Central College at 14 in 1879 and graduated in 1882; the infobox lists a Bachelor of Arts.

phases.label: President, died after 31 days
phases.summary: Elected in 1840 and died on April 4, 1841, 31 days into his term, the first president to die in office.

health.basis: Fell ill about three weeks after his inauguration and died April 4, 1841, aged 68, in the White House (infobox lists enteric fever).

position.basis: President of the United States, March 4 to April 4, 1841.

education.basis: Three years at Hampden-Sydney College, then studied medicine at the University of Pennsylvania under Benjamin Rush; left for lack of funds and is listed as a non-graduate alumnus.

misconduct.basis: No impeachment, censure or official finding is recorded for his presidency (Congress's 1814 inquiry into his army resignation found it justified, outside this phase).

phases.label: Federal judge, Governor-General of the Philippines, Secretary of War
phases.summary: Sixth Circuit judge from 1892, civilian governor of the Philippines from 1900/01 and Secretary of War from 1904, before the presidential nomination.

position.basis: Judge of the US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit 1892-1900, Governor-General of the Philippines, Secretary of War 1904-1908 (cabinet-level, below head of government).

education.basis: BA Yale 1878 (second in a class of 121) and LLB Cincinnati Law School 1880.

phases.label: President of the United States
phases.summary: One term marked by a record number of antitrust suits, the Sixteenth Amendment sent to the states, the Ballinger-Pinchot conservation dispute and a split with Roosevelt.

health.basis: Weight peaked at 335-340 lb near the end of his presidency (244 lb by 1929); he kept a daily weight record and was under a weight-loss regimen with a British physician. Documented weight concern, no diagnosis cited.

social.basis: Mixed: 70 Sherman Act suits in four years, Standard Oil and American Tobacco rulings for the government in 1911, Postal Savings System; but his 'Southern Policy' removed most Black office-holders in the South and the Mann-Elkins Act extended regulation only modestly.

position.basis: Head of state and government, 4 March 1909 - 4 March 1913.

misconduct.basis: The congressional inquiry into the Ballinger-Pinchot affair cleared Interior Secretary Ballinger by majority vote; Taft belatedly admitted a Wickersham report had been backdated. No finding against Taft himself.

phases.label: Chief Justice of the United States
phases.summary: Presided over the Taft Court, reformed federal court procedure and pushed for a Supreme Court building until failing health forced his resignation.

health.basis: By late January 1930 he could barely speak and was hallucinating; resigned 3 February 1930 and died 8 March 1930 aged 72 (heart disease, liver inflammation, high blood pressure likely).

social.basis: Mixed record: Judiciary Act of 1925 cut the case backlog and Stafford v. Wallace upheld stockyard regulation, but Bailey v. Drexel Furniture struck down a child-labor tax 8-1 and he dissented when Adkins struck down a women's minimum wage.

position.basis: Head of the federal judiciary: Senate confirmed 61-4 on 30 June 1921, sworn in 11 July 1921; the only person to be both president and chief justice.

phases.label: US Representative and Governor of Ohio
phases.summary: Congressional tariff leader (Ways and Means chair 1889-91) and governor of Ohio 1892-96.

position.basis: Governor of Ohio January 1892 - January 1896, after 14 years in the US House and chairing Ways and Means 1889-91.

education.basis: One year at Allegheny College (1860, left due to illness) and under a year at Albany Law School (1866-67) before admission to the bar in 1867.

phases.label: President of the United States
phases.summary: Economic recovery, Dingley Tariff, the Gold Standard Act and the Spanish-American War with the acquisition of the Philippines, until his assassination in September 1901.

health.basis: Shot by Leon Czolgosz on 6 September 1901; died 14 September 1901 of gangrene from infection of the wound.

social.basis: Spanish-American War: 278,000 served and seven soldiers died of disease for each killed in combat; Philippines acquired and the independence rebellion suppressed; Hawaii annexed. Little domestic social legislation.

economic.basis: Unemployment fell from nearly 20% (1895) to 15% (1897) and 8% (early 1898) as the depression ended in late 1896; Dingley Tariff raised rates (cost of living up as much as 25% by some figures); Gold Standard Act 1900. Recovery largely began before his term.

position.basis: Head of state and government 4 March 1897 - 14 September 1901.

education.basis: Allegheny College (one year) and Albany Law School (under a year).

phases.label: President of Princeton and Governor of New Jersey
phases.summary: Academic reformer at Princeton, then reform governor of New Jersey from January 1911.

health.basis: In 1906 he woke blind in the left eye from a blood clot with hypertension; modern medical opinion surmises a stroke, and arteriosclerosis was later diagnosed.

position.basis: President of Princeton University 1902-1910 and Governor of New Jersey 1911-1913.

education.basis: AB Princeton 1879; PhD in history and government, Johns Hopkins 1886 (the only president with a PhD).

phases.label: President of the United States
phases.summary: Federal Reserve, income tax and antitrust legislation, World War I, the failed League of Nations fight and the 1919 stroke.

health.basis: Stroke on 2 October 1919 left him paralysed on the left side with partial vision; he was sequestered with his wife and physician Cary Grayson and Edith Wilson managed the office; neurosurgeon Bert Park later documented impaired judgment.

social.basis: Mixed to negative: Adamson Act (eight-hour railway day, 1916), Keating-Owen Child Labor Act (struck down 1918) and the Nineteenth Amendment passed Congress in 1919; but he escalated segregation of federal offices from 1913 and the Espionage and Sedition Acts and Palmer Raids suppressed dissent. APSA 2018 ranks him 10th, C-SPAN 2017 11th.

economic.basis: Federal Reserve Act (system operating 1915 with 12 banks), 1913 income tax and Underwood tariff cut (40% to 26%); wartime budget rose from $1B (FY1916) to $19B (FY1919), prices doubled, then a 1920-21 recession with 11.9% unemployment.

position.basis: Head of state and government 4 March 1913 - 4 March 1921.

phases.label: President, died in office
phases.summary: Sixteen months in office; urged California and New Mexico to seek statehood, ratified the Clayton-Bulwer Treaty and died in July 1850.

health.basis: Plagued by gastrointestinal illness on the 1849 Northeastern tour; died in the White House on July 9, 1850, aged 65, of a 'stomach disease' about 16 months into his term.

position.basis: President of the United States, March 1849 to July 1850.

education.basis: Attended a school run by Elisha Ayer and an academy run by Kean O'Hara; formal schooling was sporadic and he did not attend college.

misconduct.basis: In the Galphin affair his Secretary of War George Crawford, the Attorney General and the Treasury Secretary settled a claim in which Crawford kept $94,176. The article reports no committee finding and does not implicate Taylor himself.

phases.label: LVMH chairman and chief executive
phases.summary: Won control of Boussac (Christian Dior) in 1984, helped form LVMH in 1987 and has chaired its executive board since 13 January 1989; the group became the world's largest luxury company and he topped the Forbes list in 2021.

position.basis: Chairman and CEO of LVMH since 1989 and chairman of Christian Dior SE.

education.basis: Studied civil engineering and mathematics at the Ecole Polytechnique, finishing in 1971; the page does not state the degree, so the score assumes the standard ingenieur-level diploma.

phases.label: Microsoft co-founder and CEO
phases.summary: Left Harvard in 1975 to co-found Microsoft and led it as CEO for about 25 years until Steve Ballmer succeeded him in 2000; the US v. Microsoft antitrust case produced findings against the company in 1999-2000.

wealth.basis: Forbes ranked him the world's wealthiest person for 13 consecutive years from 1995 to 2007; he briefly exceeded $100 billion in 1999. Federal Reserve top-0.1% household cutoff was about $45.8 million in Q3 2022 (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/WFRBLTP1311).

position.basis: Co-founder, CEO, and from 1981 chairman of Microsoft, then the dominant PC software company.

education.basis: Enrolled at Harvard in autumn 1973 and dropped out in 1975 without a degree (honorary degrees not counted).

phases.label: Foundation co-chair and technology adviser
phases.summary: Co-chaired the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation from 2000 to 2024, remained Microsoft chairman until February 2014 and left its board in 2020; the foundation became a major funder of Gavi, polio and malaria programmes.

social.basis: Gates Foundation contributed US$1,552 million (about 17.6%) of Gavi's 2016-2020 funding and pledged US$1.6 billion for 2021-2025; Gavi reports it has immunised over 760 million children and prevented over 13 million deaths. Attribution to the foundation is partial and the page also records criticism of influence over WHO funding and technology-fix approaches, so judgement is mixed-to-beneficial.

wealth.basis: Forbes estimated $106.5 billion in July 2026 and ranked him wealthiest in 18 of the 24 years 1995-2017; far above the Federal Reserve top-0.1% cutoff (about $45.8 million, Q3 2022).

position.basis: Co-chair of the world's largest private charitable foundation (endowment about $89 billion in 2025) and, until February 2014, chairman of Microsoft.

misconduct.basis: 1 documented matter(s) in the reviewed legal record, counted as the misconduct meter counts them.

phases.label: Tesla and SpaceX chief executive
phases.summary: Tesla CEO from 2008 (chairman until May 2020) and SpaceX CEO and chief engineer since its 2002 founding. In 2018 the SEC sued over a 'funding secured' tweet; he settled, paying $20 million and leaving the Tesla chair for three years.

position.basis: CEO of Tesla (from 2008) and of SpaceX; top executive of two large, high-profile companies.

education.basis: University of Pennsylvania awarded a BA in physics and a BS in economics (Wharton) in 1997; accepted at Stanford for graduate study in 1995 but did not enroll.

misconduct.basis: September 2018: the SEC sued over his tweet claiming funding was secured to take Tesla private; settled within two days without admitting or denying, with $20 million fines on Musk and on Tesla and a three-year bar from the Tesla chair. One regulator action in the phase.

phases.label: Twitter/X owner and DOGE head
phases.summary: Bought Twitter in October 2022, led the Department of Government Efficiency as a special government employee (20 Jan - 30 May 2025) and became the world's richest person; faced several SEC and court proceedings.

wealth.basis: Forbes estimates $1.1 trillion (October 2026) and has ranked him the richest person since 2025; the Federal Reserve's minimum cutoff for the top 0.1% of US households was about $45.8 million in Q3 2022 (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/WFRBLTP1311).

position.basis: CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, owner of X, de facto head of DOGE in 2025.
